### Triage summary

This is a confirmed bug: Altair `mark_geoshape()` charts render as an empty plot in Streamlit even though they display correctly in native Altair. The community discussion narrows it down to how Streamlit handles chart data: inline GeoJSON/TopoJSON geometry (and, as the reporter noticed, data pulled in via `transform_lookup`) gets dropped, so the shapes have nothing to draw.

**Likely root cause:** When converting an Altair chart to a Vega-Lite spec, Streamlit installs a custom data transformer (`_to_arrow_dataset` in `lib/streamlit/elements/vega_charts.py`) that serializes every inline dataset to Arrow IPC bytes via `convert_anything_to_arrow_bytes()`. Geometry / nested GeoJSON structures don't round-trip through a tabular Arrow/DataFrame representation — the geometry (`coordinates`, `features`, etc.) is flattened or lost during serialization — so `mark_geoshape` ends up with no geometry to render. This matches the observation that a chart defined purely by a remote data URL renders, while inline/GeoPandas geometry does not.

### Related Issues

- [#1002 - Add support for geometry dtype in `st.altair_chart`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/1002) — Directly linked in this thread; same underlying limitation that geometry data types aren't supported by Streamlit's Arrow-based chart data serialization.
- [#6099 - `st.altair_chart` removes data from a compound plot with interaction that works with `altair`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6099) — Same class of bug where data is dropped for charts with transforms/interactions, consistent with the reporter finding that `transform_lookup` triggers the empty render.

This is a well-specified enhancement (not a bug or duplicate) to make `st.login()` sessions resistant to cookie replay. Today Streamlit stores identity in a signed `_streamlit_user` cookie with a hardcoded 30-day lifetime (`AUTH_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`). The cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=lax, but there is no server-side session store, so a copied cookie remains valid on another machine until expiry, and `st.logout()` only clears cookies in the current browser. The request is an opt-in `[auth]` flag that uses Chrome’s Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC): register a device public key, issue a short-lived `__Host-` bound cookie, refresh it with a hardware-backed signature, and reject WebSocket connects when a bound identity cookie is present without the bound cookie. The sketch stays in the Starlette auth layer (`starlette_auth_routes.py` / `starlette_websocket.py`) and embeds the key thumbprint in the existing signed cookie so multi-replica deploys stay stateless. Browsers without DBSC ignore the registration header, so this can degrade cleanly if it stays off by default. Open implementation points: WebSocket upgrade vs. DBSC refresh is underspecified; new cookies must be added to Community Cloud’s forwarded-cookie allowlist; and `__Host-` cookies require HTTPS.

### Related Issues

- [#10161](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10161) — Request to make the auth cookie TTL configurable. That is the main mitigation available today (shorten the stolen-cookie window) and is complementary, not a substitute for device binding.
- [#13773](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13773) — Auth currently relies on process-local OAuth state and session affinity across replicas. This proposal’s “store the thumbprint in the signed cookie” design is meant to keep DBSC compatible with that stateless cookie model.
- [#12518](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12518) — Large OIDC payloads already force `_streamlit_user` cookie chunking and can break login. Extra bound cookies plus thumbprint data would need to stay small so they do not worsen those header/cookie-size failures.

This is a real Components V2 race, not identity churn and almost certainly not `_pending_resets`. With an explicit `key`, the element id stays stable (`key_as_main_identity=True`), but `useHandleJsContent` still re-runs the default export whenever `data` changes. A mount-time `setTriggerValue` then has to win a one-shot delivery race: the value is stored under the synthetic trigger-aggregator id (`$$STREAMLIT_INTERNAL_KEY_<id>__events`), flushed on `setTimeout(0)`, deleted from client widget state, and cleared again by `_reset_triggers()` at the end of every script run.

That aggregator id is not in the render tree, so `removeInactiveWidgetState()` on `ScriptFinished` can delete a pending trigger before the macrotask flush sends it. `_coalesce_widget_states` also preserves `trigger_value` / `chat_input_value` across queued reruns but not `json_trigger_value`, so a second widget-update message can overwrite a just-queued CCv2 trigger. Both fit the controls: `setStateValue` lives on the element id and persists; event-handler triggers fire after the app has settled. `_pending_resets` is page-scope persist-state tracking and is not involved in this repro.

Mount-time triggers are still a poor fit for Streamlit's model (use `setStateValue` for init data), but silent ~25% loss with a stable key is a bug, not intended discard-on-re-register.

### Related Issues

- [#14710](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14710) — Parent investigation this was split from. Most of that report is by-design (unkeyed `data` in identity, trigger reset after each run, first-run empty result). This issue is the remaining genuine drop with a stable `key`.
- [#8041](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8041) — Older Components V1 “not ready on first load / retry” request. Same class of mount-time value timing, different API.
- [#10102](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10102) — Another execution-model race around reruns and widget values (`fastReruns` / delayed script). Not CCv2-specific, but the same “in-flight rerun vs widget state” family.

Sorry @whitphx, I forgot to answer to this issue (mostly because I didn't have an elegant answer). 

Stremalit cache primitives work with sync functions, you couldn't decorate an async function, but:
you can call an async operation inside a cached function in separate thread (to have isolated event loop):

This should work correctly, and the result should be very close to what you want:


```python
import asyncio
import streamlit as st
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


@st.cache_data
def get_data(x:int) -> int:
    # Use a separate thread to run the async operation
    # This lets us create an isolated event loop that won't conflict
    def run_in_thread(x:int) -> int:
        async def _async_operation(x:int) -> int:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
            return x ** 2

        return asyncio.run(_async_operation(x))

    # Execute in a separate thread and wait for the result
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor:
        return executor.submit(run_in_thread, x).result()


async def main():
    x = st.slider("Pick a number" , 0, 10)
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    data = get_data(x)  # Synchronous call
    st.write(data)


asyncio.run(main())

```

Internally it uses `st.cache_data` to cache a sync function waiting for `asyncio.run(the_real_async_fun())` result in an executor thread. Similar to the pattern mentioned in other comments.

This is a follow-on enhancement, not a bug: after PR #16168 caches the awaited result of an `async def`, `st.cache_resource` still cannot safely reuse live event-loop-bound objects (async DB/HTTP/LLM clients) across reruns. Script runs typically drive asyncio with short-lived loops (`asyncio.run()`), so a cached client stays bound to a loop that is closed on the next rerun and fails with errors such as `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed`. Supporting this would need a persistent owning loop, affinity for later operations, global vs session scope, cleanup, concurrency, and reconnect behavior—beyond awaiting a coroutine and storing its return value. Workarounds (create/use/close in one coroutine, cache inert results, use sync clients, or manage a long-lived loop) are documented; `status:unlikely` matches that this is deferred pending stronger demand.

### Related Issues

- [#8308](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8308) — Original request for async `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`. #16168 covers caching inert awaited values; this issue is the remaining live-resource lifecycle case.
- [#12076](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12076) — Confirmed `Event loop is closed` when a cached LangGraph async stream is reused after the first interaction; a concrete failure of caching loop-bound resources.
- [#8488](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8488) — Native asyncio support. Persistent event-loop ownership (the main prerequisite here) is part of that broader runtime work.

This is an enhancement request to add spacing arguments on `st.divider()` so callers can control the distance to neighboring elements. Today `st.divider()` only accepts `width`; it is implemented as a markdown horizontal rule (`---`) with a hardcoded `hr` margin of `2em 0`, then stacked with the parent container’s flex `gap`. That combination is why standalone dividers often look uneven or too large compared with an in-markdown `---`. This is not a duplicate of the default-spacing papercut, but it is motivated by the same visual problem. Existing workarounds include wrapping content in a container with a custom `gap`, or pairing `st.divider()` with `st.space()`, neither of which replaces the rule’s own margins.

I think that this could be solved by having an invalidation callback. If the callback returns true, the fragment is invalidated and re-rendered. This would allow for you to check for changes in session state that impact the fragment.

Here is a really simple example using a counter. In a more complex application, there might be many places that increment the count that exist outside the fragments which display it.

```python
import streamlit as st

def invalidator():
    if st.session_state['prev'] != st.session_state['current']
        st.session_state['prev'] = st.session_state['current']
        return true
    return false

def increment_value():
    st.session_state['current'] = st.session_state['current'] + 1

@st.experimental_fragment(invalidation_callback=invalidator)
def display_value():
    st.print(st.session_state['current'])

if st.session_state.get('current') == None:
    st.session_state['current'] = 0

st.button('Increment Value', on_click=increment_value)
display_value()
```

@vdonato that is a _really_ good question and I have a two part answer/opinion.

1. I think that the behavior you've gone with _is_ reasonable, and your logic is sound.
2. This unfortunately means (I think) that the `fragment` mechanism won't do what I was originally hoping it _could_ do.

To explain #2, here is a simplified version of the code that I was _hoping_ would be enabled by allowing you to re-run fragments programatically.

```python
@st.experimental_fragment
def a_simple_counter():
    current_count = st.session_state.counter

    st.write("The counter is at", current_count)
    if current_count < 10:
       time.sleep(1)
       st.session_state.counter += 1
       st.rerun(scope="fragment")
    else:
       st.button("Reset Counter", on_click=reset_counter)
       st.success("Finished")

def reset_counter():
    st.session_state.counter = 0


# Page code
reset_counter()
a_simple_counter()
st.button("rerun-page", help="just a button to click to force a full rerun")
```

If the behavior of `st.rerun(scope="fragment")` is as you have described above, then every time the _full page_ re-runs,
the counter will sleep for 1 second, increment the counter by 1, and then do nothing since the rerun is skipped. Only by clicking the "Reset Counter" button _inside of the fragment_ will it trigger a fragment-rerun that causes the fragment to count to 10 before it completes and ceases to run.

In my ideal world, when the fragment is first encountered during a full page re-run, it would start running in it's own separate script thread and continue to re-run itself, updating it's little block of the page until the counter reaches 10. Almost like a thread spawn. Meanwhile, the rest of the script _continues_ to run until it reaches the end of the main page. This is not how I think you guys originally envisioned `fragments` to work. For fairly obvious reasons this would have all the race-conditiony fun and joy of dealing with threaded concurrency. I am not saying you should make fragments do this.

Now, the behavior where `st.rerun(scope="fragment")` queues up the fragment to be "rerun" _after_ the main script execution **would actually solve my problem here**. Once the page code finishes, the fragment would resume counting from wherever it left off until it reached 10, whereupon it too would exit. However I can, as you likely did, envision many other uses for `fragment` where this behavior would not be expected and potentially even cause major issues or confusion. It leaves major questions open like "what if a `rerun` is encountered multiple times in the fragment"? 

You could make the "scheduled execution" opt-in via a second argument; `st.rerun(scope="fragment", when="soon")` perhaps. This could have the behavior of causing the rerun of the page/fragment to be scheduled "soon" (e.g. as soon as possible after the current thing that is running finishes, similar to how scheduling things "soon" in async code works). I don't know that that would be easy to implement, though, and would definitely have to get run by product team separately.

This is a keyboard regression in `st.multiselect` after the BaseWeb → React Aria ComboBox migration ([#16175](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16175), shipped in 1.61). RAC does not auto-focus a list item while typing (`focusedKey` stays null, no `aria-activedescendant`), so in **1.62.0** Enter is a no-op: the filter is cleared and the menu closes without selecting anything. `st.selectbox` still commits its first filtered option via a dedicated Enter handler, which is why the widgets now diverge.

**1.63.0** ([#16673](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16673)) replaced that no-op with “unfocused Enter commits the first visible row.” When two or more options match, that first row is `Select N matches` (`__select_matches__`), not the first option as in 1.49.1. Product approved this default; `select_all=False` restores type-then-Enter of the first match. Skipping the bulk row on Enter was explicitly rejected. A remaining gap is visual/ARIA highlighting: the first row is CSS-highlighted via `aria-posinset`, but RAC `focusedKey` / `aria-activedescendant` is still a TODO, so ArrowDown still lands on the bulk row first.

### Related Issues

- [#16537](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16537) — Same type-then-Enter vs “Select N matches” request. Closed by [#16673](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16673), which added `select_all=False` as the opt-out that restores first-match Enter.
- [#16003](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16003) — Cited by the reporter. Another quiet behavior loss from the React Aria ComboBox migration (selectbox fuzzy search), same class of regression.
- [#15697](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15697) — Open enhancement for customizable selectbox/multiselect keyboard navigation; related interaction surface, not a duplicate of this Enter/filter bug.

`st.download_button` serves files from the media endpoint, which builds `Content-Disposition` in `_media_endpoint` (`lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py`). Latin-1-encodable names are interpolated as `filename="{filename}"` with no escaping; only non-latin-1 names take the RFC 5987 `filename*=utf-8''{quote(filename)}` form. A `"` is latin-1, so names like `5" x 7" print.jpg` emit `attachment; filename="5" x 7" print.jpg"`, which is not a valid RFC 6266 header and causes the browser to save the wrong name. The same path also accepts inferred names from file objects (since 1.61.0 / #14159), so this is not limited to an explicit `file_name=`. Existing tests cover the utf-8 branch and a space-containing quoted name, but not `"`. The latin-1 vs utf-8 split was added in #5465 to fix #5434; the missing piece is treating quoted-string-unsafe characters the way Starlette's `FileResponse` does (`quote(filename) == filename`).

### Related Issues

- [#5434](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5434) (closed) — Non-latin-1 `file_name` values crashed header encoding. PR [#5465](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/5465) added the latin-1 / `filename*=` split that this report shows is too narrow.
- [#5566](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5566) (closed) — Docs discussion of RFC 6266 filename handling for `st.download_button`. Explicit `file_name` values are still passed through without escaping at the header boundary.
- [#14159](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14159) — Infer `file_name` from file-like `data.name`. That inference is now landed, so uploaded / on-disk names (which can contain `"`) also reach this header.

No duplicate of this specific quoted-string bug was found.

I took a look at this and wanted to share my findings.

The behavior has described in the ticket is correct, thank you @cboettig for a great issue report!

In the code, we've had a [long-standing statement](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/500b739c0d3cd623849ba986e390630db793b853/frontend/src/components/elements/DeckGlJsonChart/DeckGlJsonChart.tsx#L76) that intentionally removes views from being passed to deck.gl on the frontend since we've traditionally just supported a single MapView.

Deck.gl has 4 fully supported views (MapView, FirstPersonView, OrthographicView, OrbitView), and 1 experimental view (_GlobeView) [[docs](https://deck.gl/docs/developer-guide/views)]. In order to support all of these view types, we'd need to do a bit of refactoring that adds support for all the different types of views. We may even want to consider supporting multiple types of views at once, since Deck.gl supports this too.

If we were to fix this, this is a potentially breaking change for apps that may have previously passed in a pydeck View, but rely on it falling back to MapView at runtime. 

```python
st.pydeck_chart(
    pdk.Deck(
        views=[pdk.View(type="FirstPersonView")],
        # Other args...
    )
)
```

To be clear, that certainly isn't a reason _against_ fixing this as we'd be technically fixing that issue as well during this, I'm just using this to illustrate the compounding factors that are at hand with this.

With all of that said, I am going to turn this into a feature request given the breadth of what may need to be done in order to support this!

This is a feature request for a new `st.sandbox()` API that would execute LLM-generated Streamlit Python (charts, maps, etc.) inside an app, with an allowlist of packages and structured `success` / `error` / `security_violation` results. The motivating use case is chatbot/data-agent dashboards: static helper functions are too rigid, and rendering LLM HTML via `st.html` does not pick up Streamlit theming. Streamlit has no sandboxed nested-exec API today; app scripts are run with process-level `exec()` in the script runner, and an e2e fixture already demonstrates the unsafe pattern of parsing Python from a chat response and `exec()`-ing it inside an `@st.fragment`. True isolation would need more than an import allowlist (RestrictedPython-style checks are easy to bypass); likely options are a nested runtime, process isolation, or in-browser WASM execution.

### Related Issues

- [#12991](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12991) — AI-assisted chart builder: same “LLM produces a visualization” goal, but it would generate Vega/Plotly specs rather than execute arbitrary Streamlit Python.
- [#16305](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16305) — Official Pyodide/WASM support (and community `stlite`): a plausible way to run untrusted Streamlit code in the browser instead of on the app server.
- [#7546](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7546) — Multiple `Runtime` instances in one process: needed to host isolated Streamlit environments, which a nested sandbox would likely depend on.

This is a follow-on enhancement, not a bug: allow `refresh_mode="background"` on async `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource` functions. PR #16168 (implementing #8308) adds foreground async caching but rejects this combination at decoration time. That is consistent with the current design — `cache_background_refresh.py` runs work as a synchronous `Callable[[], None]` on a bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor`, so it cannot await a coroutine or own an event loop. Shipping this needs explicit semantics for loop ownership, cancellation/errors, same-key refresh deduplication, and discarding late results after cache/session invalidation. Until then, async cached functions should keep using `refresh_mode="foreground"`.

### Related Issues

- [#8308](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8308) — Parent request for async `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`. This issue is a scoped follow-up for background refresh, not a duplicate of foreground async caching.
- [#8645](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8645) — Original request for serving a stale cache value while refreshing in the background (the sync `refresh_mode="background"` feature this would extend to coroutines).
- [#6687](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6687) — Related request to run slow work off the script rerun so the app stays responsive; overlaps the “don’t block on refresh” motivation, but is a broader background-task API rather than TTL cache refresh.

Confirmed: `uploadFileUploaderFile` in `frontend/connection/src/DefaultStreamlitEndpoints.ts` builds the multipart body with `form.append(name, file, fileName)`, so the user-controlled `File.name` becomes the form-data field name while the real filename/path is already passed separately as the third argument. The backend does not use that field name — `_upload_put` in `starlette_routes.py` collects whichever `UploadFile` is present and stores `upload.filename` — and its tests already default to `name="file"`. This is defense-in-depth rather than a Streamlit-native injection: the field name is unused for routing, storage, or auth, but putting unsanitized filenames into `Content-Disposition` `name=` can still trip WAFs, proxies, or multipart parsers. The proposed `form.append("file", file, fileName)` matches the backend and also covers `st.chat_input`, `st.camera_input`, and `st.audio_input`, which share this upload path.

### Related Issues

- [#8544](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8544) — Server-side `DecodeError` on uploads with unusual filenames (e.g. double extensions). Same theme: user-controlled filename strings in the multipart `Content-Disposition` header causing unexpected parse/error behavior.
- [#11396](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11396) (closed) — Uploads with Unicode filenames failing with HTTP 400 on Community Cloud. Using the filename as the form field name (not only as `filename=`) can add extra encoding/parser pressure; a static field name would isolate that to the intended filename parameter.
- [#10049](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10049) — `st.file_uploader` request handling behind proxies/load balancers. Related because this report’s risk is mainly intermediary (WAF/proxy) treatment of the upload payload, not Streamlit’s own file storage.

Thanks for the detailed report — confirmed in the code, and the proposed fix is the right one.

Verified:
- `frontend/connection/src/DefaultStreamlitEndpoints.ts` does `form.append(name, file, fileName)`, so the user-controlled `File.name` becomes the multipart field name.
- The backend genuinely doesn't need it: `_upload_put` in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py` collects uploads via `form.values()` and stores `upload.filename`. It's the only server-side consumer of the form, and our existing route tests already build bodies with `name="file"` — so switching to a static field name is a no-op server-side.
- The same upload path is shared by `st.file_uploader`, `st.chat_input`, `st.camera_input`, and `st.audio_input`, so the change covers all of them at once.

One scoping note on the security framing: we don't think this is exploitable against Streamlit itself. The field name isn't used for routing, storage, or auth, and browsers percent-encode `"`, CR, and LF in `FormData` entry names as part of the multipart/form-data serialization algorithm — so a filename can't inject header structure into the request. What's left is real but defense-in-depth: unbounded length and arbitrary charsets in a field name can create avoidable friction with WAFs, proxies, and stricter multipart parsers in front of an app. This behavior also dates back to 1.26 (#7025), so it isn't a regression.

So we're treating it as hardening rather than a vulnerability — low priority, but worth doing since the change is a one-liner with no behavioral impact, and it keeps user-controlled data confined to the `filename` parameter where it belongs.

Following up on my earlier comment: I said the proposed fix was right, and as a code change it is — but we implemented it, measured it, and decided not to make the change.

What a receiver actually sees, in Chromium, for the filename `ev"il\r\n.txt`:

```
before: name="ev%22il%0D%0A.txt"; filename="ev%22il%0D%0A.txt"
after:  name="file";              filename="ev%22il%0D%0A.txt"
```

So there's no injection vector: browsers percent-encode `"`, CR, and LF in both parameters, so a filename can't add a second `name` or break the header. And the change doesn't remove the exposure, only a duplicate of it — the same string still reaches the same header via `filename`, which the server needs in order to name the file, so a WAF or strict parser that rejects an unusual filename rejects it either way. The field name itself is never used for routing, storage, or auth.

Against that near-zero benefit: uploads can be redirected to host-provided endpoints that parse this body outside this repo. A receiver taking the filename from the field name would silently name every upload `file`, and nothing in our CI could catch it — Chromium doesn't expose a file-bearing multipart body to Playwright, so those bytes aren't assertable end-to-end.

If a WAF, proxy, or gateway actually rejects or mangles a Streamlit upload because of the field name — a rule that fired, a request that failed — that would change the calculus; please reopen with those details. Thanks for the careful write-up.

This is a confirmed bug related to Streamlit's execution model and asyncio event loop handling. The root cause is that Streamlit's `ScriptRunner` creates a dedicated thread (`ScriptRunner.scriptThread`) to execute user scripts, but this thread does not have an asyncio event loop associated with it. When Python code calls `asyncio.get_event_loop()` from a thread without a running event loop (especially in Python 3.10+), it raises `RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread`. This affects any library that depends on asyncio (like pyppeteer, playwright, aiohttp, etc.).

The workaround is to manually create a new event loop in the script thread using `asyncio.new_event_loop()` and `asyncio.set_event_loop()`, but a proper fix would require Streamlit to either set up an event loop for the ScriptRunner thread or provide native async/await support.

`mapbox.token` was deprecated in #11231 with `expiration_date="2026-05-01"`. That date is now in the past, so `ConfigOption.is_expired()` is true and setting the option logs **ERROR** `IS NO LONGER SUPPORTED`. Expiration only changes the log text: the option is still registered, still readable via `config.get_option("mapbox.token")`, and still applied in `st.map`, `st.pydeck_chart`, and `_fix_pydeck_mapbox_api_warning()` (which copies it into `MAPBOX_API_KEY`). Unit tests still assert the token is forwarded to the proto. There is no CI check that a deprecated option’s expiration date has passed, so this drifted without a corresponding removal. Fix is to either remove the option (and stop reading it) or push the expiration date so the message matches current behavior.

For the 502 Error regarding the login issue check nginx header size limits. That fixed the problem for me! 

```
Request headers (browser -> Nginx):
client_header_buffer_size
large_client_header_buffers

Response headers (upstream -> Nginx, e.g., large Set-Cookie):
proxy_buffer_size
proxy_buffers
```

This issue reports three related regressions since Streamlit 1.53, all stemming from two PRs that shipped in that release: **"Expose OIDC tokens" (#12044)** and **"Make st.logout use end_session_endpoint" (#12693)**.

**1. 502 Bad Gateway on Kubernetes/NGINX:** The new token exposure feature introduced cookie chunking (`_streamlit_user_tokens` split into multiple cookies) plus a second cookie for tokens. NGINX Ingress controllers have default `proxy_buffer_size` (4K) and `large_client_header_buffers` (8K) limits. Multiple signed, chunked `Set-Cookie` headers can exceed these limits, causing NGINX to return 502. The "Split cookie into 2 chunks" log message confirms this is happening. Users behind reverse proxies may need to increase their buffer sizes, but Streamlit should also consider minimizing cookie overhead.

**2. Logout account selection prompt:** Before 1.53, `st.logout()` simply cleared the local auth cookie and redirected to the app root. Now it redirects to the OIDC provider's `end_session_endpoint`, which many providers (especially Microsoft/Azure AD) use to display an account selection screen. While this was an intentional change (to properly end provider sessions per the OIDC RP-Initiated Logout spec), it changes the UX. Passing the `id_token_hint` should in theory suppress the account picker on compliant providers, but not all providers handle this consistently.

**3. "Split cookie" log message:** This is expected INFO-level logging from the new cookie chunking logic in `auth_util.py` (line 420) and is not a bug, though the log level could arguably be lowered to DEBUG to avoid noise.

### Related Issues

- **#13773** — [Google Auth does not work with multiple replicas](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13773): Also involves auth failures in Kubernetes deployments. The in-memory `auth_cache` (used for OAuth state) is not shared across replicas, compounding deployment-related auth problems.
- **#12518** — [st.login fails for users with large number of AD Groups](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12518): The cookie chunking mechanism was partly introduced to fix this issue (large user info exceeding cookie limits), but the additional cookies and chunks can now cause problems with reverse proxy header size limits.
- **#11900** (closed) — [st.logout does not end the session with the OIDC provider](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11900): This was the original request that led to the `end_session_endpoint` redirect in `st.logout()`, which is now causing the account selection prompt reported here.

Hi. I'm the contributor that wrote the logout code as it currently stands.

The one thing that became pretty clear is that there is a LOT of heterogeneity in how OAuth providers work, and that the standard is taken at best as a loose set of guidelines. For instance, many providers require extra parameters on the loguout query that are clearly labeled as optional in standards (description of https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/12693 covers these cases with links to bug reports from the first time I tried implementing it). 

So in response to the question
> Is there a way to specify which OAuth token you want to logout of?

Yes, there is, the token is being passed to the logout request and the provider is not doing anything with it. And that is to be expected considering the heterogeneity (and to a degree, vagueness of the standard on what the logout should actually do). 

Now for context: 
What logout did pre 1.53.0 is it just deleted the session auth cookie for streamlit. So next time you logged in, login flow would get called again. Which for many OIDC providers (such as Frontegg which is what we are using) just automatically succeeds if a cookie for the provider is still present. And it is, because that is only cleared when calling the logout endpoint.  Effectively for us, logout did functionally nothing pre 1.53.

So, unfortunately, fixing it for me broke it for you. So I apologise and sympathise. 

I believe the best way forward is more configuration. Most notably, the ability to turn off the logout redirect via .secrets [auth] configuration, which should be very straightforward to implement and should effectively restore the pre 1.53 state for those for whom that was better. 

As for the original issue and https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14331 - I believe the fix, while technically solving the issue for now, is fundamentally misguided. Assuming you eventually want to implement token refresh https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/12696#issuecomment-3861008419, which I assume you will as short-lived access tokens is an increasingly common pattern for OIDC providers, you will need to be storing the refresh token, running head-first into the same header issues as here. So I'd say the correct response is documenting the behavior and saying you should configure your http server to accept large headers as in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14290#issuecomment-4030052450 (as it seems to be on average a rare'ish occurrence)

Or, for an even more concrete reason why removing tokens is not a good fix:  even the ID token itself is technically unbounded in size and can blow past the header size limits: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12518

I spent some time measuring where the auth cookie bytes actually go, since the discussion above turns on that question. Sharing the numbers in case they are useful.

**Method.** `TestClient` driving the real Starlette auth routes and the real signer, with a `groups` claim of N sha256 hexdigests — incompressible enough that the zlib pass inside `itsdangerous` does not flatter the result. Sizes are the request `Cookie` header the browser sends back, which is what `large_client_header_buffers` and `proxy_buffer_size` actually limit. Note that no tokens are stored in these runs: everything below comes from the identity cookie alone.

## 1. The header is claim values and almost nothing else

| claim | cookies | request `Cookie` header | values | names + separators |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 400 groups | 12 | 21,474 B | 21,242 B | 232 B |
| 100 groups | 5 | 5,627 B | 5,529 B | 98 B |

98% of the header is claim values. Two consequences for the fixes discussed above:

- Changing how the cookie is split, named or packed can only ever recover the last column — 232 bytes out of 21,474. I built a version that packs the chunks to the byte and measured it; the header moved by 1.5%. There is no variant of that idea that matters.
- These figures were produced with **no tokens stored at all**. Making token exposure opt-in (#14331) therefore cannot bound the header either: at 100 groups, the identity cookie alone already exceeds the 4 KB `proxy_buffer_size` default before a single token is added. That is the same ceiling @velochy pointed at, measured.

If the goal is to get under NGINX's defaults, the only lever with enough range is carrying fewer claims — or not carrying them in a cookie at all.

## 2. A separate bug found along the way: orphaned chunks are never cleared

A chunked auth cookie is a main cookie holding the count plus `{name}_1`, `{name}_2`, … siblings. When a later login produces fewer chunks than an earlier one, the surplus siblings are never removed: they carry a valid signature, so `_clear_invalid_auth_cookies` — which only fires for cookies that fail signature validation — leaves them in place. They persist for the full 30-day cookie lifetime and are sent on every request, including the WebSocket upgrade.

Two consecutive logins in one browser session, a large claim followed by a small one:

| | after login 1 (400 groups) | after login 2 (1 group) |
|---|---|---|
| `develop` | 12 cookies, 21,474 B | 12 cookies, 21,671 B |
| with the fix below | 12 cookies, 21,474 B | 2 cookies, 329 B |

On `develop` the header does not shrink after the second login — it grows slightly, because the main cookie reverts to holding the payload while `_streamlit_user_1` … `_streamlit_user_10` remain behind.

This matters most for #12518, which was closed on the grounds that cookies are now chunked properly. The users there resolved their problem by reconfiguring Entra to emit fewer groups, which is precisely the case that strands the earlier chunks: the app stays broken after the cause has been removed, until the user manually clears their browser cookies.

**Fix:** [`15bdbac`](https://github.com/herley-shaori/streamlit/commit/15bdbac61ee2b54de95bb05b66d71d51991ba618) on [`fix/clear-orphaned-auth-cookie-chunks`](https://github.com/herley-shaori/streamlit/tree/fix/clear-orphaned-auth-cookie-chunks), rebased on `665efd4e6`. `_set_auth_cookie` deletes the chunk siblings present in the request before writing the fresh cookies; rewritten chunks are set again afterwards and win, since the browser applies the last value for a cookie name. The sibling scan is shared with the existing clearing path. Covered by a callback-level regression test that fails on `develop` with three orphaned chunks remaining; ruff, mypy and `lib/tests/streamlit/web/server/` (771 tests) pass.

To be explicit about scope: this does **not** fix the oversized-header reports in this issue. It fixes the recovery path, which is a different problem.

This is expected behavior, not a typing bug we can fix with overloads.

`st.number_input` infers int vs float from the runtime values of `value` / `min_value` / `max_value` / `step`. A variable annotated `int | None` is just `None` at runtime, so with no other int args the widget is a float input and returns `float | None`. Type checkers follow that: the union splits into `value: int` → `int` and `value: None` → `float | None`, which is `int | float | None` (often shown as `float | None`). An overload that reported `int | None` would disagree with runtime.

Workarounds for an empty integer input:

```python
number = st.number_input("Input number", value=default_value, step=1)
# or min_value=0 / max_value=... as int
```

If you only need the annotation to be `int | None` and already know the widget is an int (e.g. you passed `step=1`):

```python
from typing import cast

number = cast(int | None, st.number_input("Input number", value=default_value, step=1))
```

`cast` alone does not change the runtime type. Without an int `step` / `min_value` / `max_value`, entered values are still floats.

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

We ended up moving off lazy `data=` entirely (eager bytes, pre-warmed at save time) because we couldn't make the callable's dependency tree provably free of session/cache reads. For anyone hitting this: if your callable calls anything that isn't a pure function of its arguments, the missing context isn't just a perf/warning issue, it's a correctness one.

Diagnosed the exact mechanism for why the clear affordance sometimes doesn't work, in case it helps whoever picks this up.

We hit this with dates loaded from a DB, some `NULL` (→ `value=None`) and some set (→ `value=date(...)`). Rows loaded with a set date could never be cleared back to empty from the UI. Checked with DevTools: it's not `min_value`, not the column width — the clear button (⊗) simply **doesn't exist in the DOM at all** unless the widget's *first* render passed `value=None`. If the first render passes an actual date, there's no clear affordance ever, even on a later rerun with `value=None`; the text-delete gesture also self-restores on blur in that case.

So the clearability seems to be decided once, at first mount, rather than being derived from the current `value` on each render. Workaround we're using: a checkbox gate ("set end date") that only mounts the `date_input` once the checkbox is on, so its first render is always the meaningful one — but a native reset button (as requested in this issue) or making the ⊗ affordance reactive to the current `value` would remove the need for that.

Adding a data point: this isn't just cosmetic desync, it can freeze an app entirely.

We had a `st.selectbox` with a "sentinel" option acting as a group separator, guarded with the standard pattern: `if selected == SENTINEL: st.session_state.pop(key); st.rerun()`. In production this caused a full livelock — the guard cleared server-side state, but the frontend `WidgetStateManager` kept re-sending the stale sentinel value on every subsequent user event, so every rerun was consumed re-triggering the same guard. No exception, no CPU loop, just a page that stopped responding to input. Two users affected, emergency rollback.

Root cause is the same one described here: deleting the key resets the *value* but not the widget's own display/selection state, so on rerun the two diverge — and in our case that divergence became self-perpetuating instead of just visually stale.

The reason we needed a sentinel option in the first place is that `st.selectbox`/`st.multiselect` have no way to mark an option as non-selectable (group header, separator). If that existed as a first-class feature, we wouldn't have needed the pop+rerun workaround at all — so this issue and a "disabled/non-selectable options" feature request are two sides of the same gap. Happy to share more repro detail if useful.

We hit this in production: an `st.selectbox` with ~16,000 options (Italian postal code + city + province, for a destination picker in an internal logistics tool). Sharing data in case it's useful for prioritization, since the [2026-03-25 selectbox-filter-mode spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-03-25-selectbox-filter-mode/product-spec.md) already lists server-side filtering for large option sets under "Future Work".

**The cost scales with option *count*, not payload size.** We isolated this with a parametric benchmark (single `st.selectbox`, nothing else):

| case | options | payload | time to interactive |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 60,000 | 1,699 KB | ~3.9–4.7 s |
| B | 60,000 | 410 KB | ~4.7 s |
| C | 17,000 | 481 KB | ~2.1 s |

A vs B: same option count, payload 4× different → times are the same. B vs C: payload roughly the same, option count 3.5× different → times differ ~2.2×. So compressing the data (shorter labels, ID-based reconstruction, tighter serialization) doesn't help — the bottleneck is rendering N options client-side, not transferring bytes.

We also tried working around it at the app level (mount the search field lazily behind a click instead of on open) — it moves the cost to a click instead of removing it, and it's worse UX (the affordance implies a ready list, the click looks like it did nothing while the payload streams in). We ended up reverting that.

Only a real fix removes the cost: server-side filtering, so the browser never receives more than a page of options at a time. Right now, sending fewer options ourselves would make the built-in fuzzy/contains search silently lie (a value outside the truncated subset would show "no results" even though it exists) — not something we want on a page that quotes prices.

Given PRs from outside the maintainer team are currently paused, not proposing an implementation here — just flagging a concrete production use case and the measurement behind it, in case it helps move this from "Future Work" up the list. Happy to share the benchmark script or more detail if useful.

Found the precise mechanism, which also explains the exact ~10KB boundary — filed against sentry-python since it's really their code path: https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/issues/7285

In short: `StarletteIntegration.patch_request_response()` wraps every route endpoint (including `_upload_put`). Before the handler runs, Sentry's `StarletteRequestExtractor.extract_request_info()` calls `await request.body()`/`.form()` whenever `content_length` is within its default `max_request_body_size` ("medium" → `content_length <= 10_000` bytes) — this fully drains the ASGI `receive()` channel purely to populate breadcrumb/event data.

`_upload_put` (`streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py`) then builds its own `StarletteRequest(request.scope, limited_receive)` to enforce a streaming size cap, where `limited_receive` calls `await request.receive()` directly — the same raw ASGI channel Sentry already drained. That second read blocks forever (no more body left, no disconnect coming on a keep-alive connection), which is the hang.

For uploads over 10,000 bytes, Sentry's size check skips body capture entirely, so the channel is untouched and the upload succeeds — matching the exact size boundary seen in testing.

This isn't really fixable from Streamlit's side alone — any ASGI middleware that reads the body first (not just Sentry) would break `_upload_put`'s manual receive the same way, since it isn't going through Starlette's own cached `Request.body()`/`.stream()`. Flagging here for visibility in case a defensive fix on this side (e.g. checking whether the body was already consumed, or reusing the original request via `Request.stream()`/cached body when available) is worth considering regardless of how the Sentry side lands.

`st.file_uploader` hangs on uploads under ~10KB when `sentry_sdk.init()` runs in the same process before Streamlit starts. Sentry’s default `StarletteIntegration` drains the ASGI body (via `request.body()` / `.form()`) for requests with `content_length <= 10_000`. `_upload_put` in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_routes.py` then wraps `request.receive()` in `limited_receive` and builds a **new** `StarletteRequest` for multipart parsing, which does not see Starlette’s cached body. The second `receive()` blocks indefinitely on a keep-alive connection. Uploads over ~10KB skip Sentry body capture, matching the reported boundary. The same `/_stcore/upload_file` route is used by `st.camera_input` and `st.chat_input` attachments. Workaround: disable `StarletteIntegration` (or avoid in-process Sentry init). A Streamlit-side defensive fix would reuse the original request’s cached body / `Request.stream()` instead of a raw second `receive()`.

### Related Issues

- [#16139](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16139) — Closed. Another in-process `sentry_sdk.init()` interaction with Streamlit (ThreadingIntegration + `st.fragment(run_every)`). Different mechanism; the reporter correctly ruled this out.
- [#15374](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15374) — Closed. Sentry/threading wrapper clash around `add_script_run_ctx` in 1.58.0. Same “Sentry instruments Streamlit in-process” class of bug, not a duplicate of this hang.
- Upstream: [getsentry/sentry-python#7285](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/issues/7285) — Reporter’s Sentry-side write-up of the body-drain + second `receive()` hang.

No open Streamlit duplicates found. Other `st.file_uploader` timeout issues (e.g. [#11419](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11419)) are unrelated client/mobile timeouts.

Confirmed, and your root-cause analysis is exactly right — thank you, the write-up made this quick to verify. Editing this comment to keep everything in one place now that we've implemented a fix; the mechanism section is unchanged, the "which middleware patterns break" characterization is corrected, and the open question about Sentry's `Request` instance is resolved.

**Mechanism**

Confirmed against Starlette 1.6.0: `Request.body()` caches into `self._body` **per instance**, and `stream()` only consults `hasattr(self, "_body")`. Because `_upload_put` constructs a *new* `StarletteRequest(request.scope, limited_receive)` whose `limited_receive` calls the raw `request.receive()`, it can never see that cache. The second read then blocks forever on a keep-alive connection. Reproduced with no `sentry_sdk` installed at all, using a stand-in that reads the request body before the handler runs:

```
CASE 1: no middleware reading the body (control)
  RESULT: completed, status=204
CASE 2: middleware reads body first (models Sentry StarletteIntegration)
  middleware pre-read 159 bytes of body
  RESULT: *** HUNG *** (timed out after 3s; receive() called 2x)
```

**It's a regression in 1.61.0**

You mentioned you hadn't tested older versions, so: the `limited_receive` pattern was introduced in #16207 ("Enforce upload size limit while streaming body"), which shipped in **1.61.0**. Before that, the handler called `await request.form()` on the *original* request, which is cache-aware. Same drained-channel scenario against the old code path:

```
OLD (pre-#16207) `await request.form()`: OK -> ['foo.txt']  (receive calls: 1)
```

So 1.60.x and earlier are unaffected, and 1.61.0 onward is broken.

**Which patterns actually break (correcting an earlier overstatement)**

An earlier version of this comment said `_upload_put` is incompatible with *any* body-reading ASGI middleware. That was too broad. Measured against a real uvicorn server with keep-alive, there are three distinct patterns, and only some break:

| Pattern | Before fix | After fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No middleware | 204 | 204 |
| Reads the body via the **same** `Request` the endpoint receives (Sentry's `StarletteIntegration`, which patches `starlette.routing.request_response`) | **hangs** | 204 |
| Buffers the body and replays it downstream (the well-behaved ASGI contract) | 204 | 204 |
| Consumes the raw channel and passes it down **without** replaying | **hangs** | **still hangs** |

The last row is not recoverable from our side — the bytes are genuinely gone, and the handler can't distinguish "no more body coming" from "body still in flight" without a disconnect. Worth flagging for anyone wrapping Streamlit in a custom ASGI stack: buffer-and-replay is safe, drain-without-replay is not, and that holds independently of this fix.

**Your open question, resolved**

Sentry does read from the same `Request` instance, so a cache-aware read is sufficient and no buffering workaround is needed. In `sentry_sdk.integrations.starlette`, `_wrap_async_handler` does `request = args[0]` and then `StarletteRequestExtractor(request)`; the extractor's `form()` deliberately calls `await self.request.body()` first (with a comment noting Starlette doesn't cache `form()` the way it caches `body()`). Verified against sentry-sdk 2.68.1. The ~10KB boundary is `request_body_within_bounds` under the default `max_request_body_size="medium"`, matching your numbers exactly.

**The fix**

`_upload_put` now reads through the original request's `stream()` — which replays Starlette's cached body when present — instead of the raw `receive()` channel, while still counting bytes to preserve #16207's streaming size cap. That cap exists to stop an oversized upload from being buffered in memory or spooled to disk before the size check runs, so we didn't want to trade this hang for that. Verified end to end against real sentry-sdk 2.68.1 + uvicorn: the sub-10KB upload that previously hung now returns 204, and the >10KB case is unchanged.

One behavior change worth noting: a body consumed without being cached now returns a clear 400 rather than hanging or surfacing an opaque 500.

**Triage**

Confirmed bug, prioritized as a regression affecting `st.file_uploader`, `st.chat_input` attachments, `st.camera_input`, and `st.audio_input` — all four share the `/_stcore/upload_file` route. The silent-hang failure mode with no error or log makes this disproportionately hard to diagnose, which we weighted in.

Thanks also for filing [getsentry/sentry-python#7285](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/issues/7285). We're fixing this on our side regardless, since that upstream fix would address one trigger rather than the pattern.

In the meantime, for anyone hitting this on 1.61.x: `disabled_integrations=[StarletteIntegration()]` in your `sentry_sdk.init()` avoids it, at the cost of Sentry's Starlette request instrumentation.

This is a bug report about Components V2 (`st.components.v2.component`) dropping `setTriggerValue` (and `setStateValue`) results when the component's JavaScript runs on initialization (mount) rather than in response to user interaction. The root cause is a timing/race condition inherent in the Streamlit execution model: the Python script finishes execution before the frontend has a chance to render the component, load its JS module (async `import()`), execute the default function, and send the trigger/state value back via `updateWidgets`. This means the component always returns an empty/default result on its first script run. The problem compounds when multiple such components are used sequentially — satisfying one triggers a rerun that resets the other, making it effectively impossible for both to return values simultaneously. The issue discussion confirms this affects both `setTriggerValue` and `setStateValue` during mount-time initialization, and multiple community members have requested a "blocking" component mode that waits for the frontend JS to execute before the backend continues.

- [#8041 - Restart app if component doesn't load](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8041): Describes the same fundamental problem for v1 components — components not being ready on first load and needing a workaround (rerun/retry). The reporter specifically notes that Components V2 should help fix this, but as this issue shows, the same timing problem persists.
- [#13671 - Allow bytes in a dict for custom components v2](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13671): Related Components V2 enhancement for data serialization. Not a duplicate, but part of the same V2 API surface area being actively developed.
- [#9422 - `Streamlit.setComponentValue` doesn't return `Set` type variables](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9422): Related to data type handling in custom component return values. Different root cause but affects the same custom component value passing path.

All measurements below are on 1.62.0:

### What reproduces

The reported symptom reproduces deterministically — the page never finishes loading, the second component never resolves, and the retry loop runs hot: **863 script runs in 15 seconds (~58 reruns/sec)**, with no error or warning surfaced.

### Why the original version never converges

`data` is hashed into the element id, so `unique_line_time()` builds a **different widget on almost every run**. The value the previous instance sent belongs to a widget that no longer exists. Measured: **0 of 1,271 runs** received a value, with 688 distinct element ids observed in 12 seconds. It works only when two runs happen to land in the same second — which is exactly the "about half the time" behaviour described above.

This is documented behaviour, in `component-v2-lib/src/types.ts`:

> If a component is mounted without a `key` parameter in Python, and one of the parameters in the mounting command changes, then this frontend key may change between app runs.

One consequence worth flagging, since avoiding `session_state` clutter was the stated reason for going unkeyed: the unkeyed version is the one that **accumulates** orphaned widget entries — registered ids grew 2 → 6 → 8 → 10 → 12 → 14 over six runs. Passing a `key` is what keeps state bounded.

### The trigger diagnosis in this thread was correct

The conclusion that trigger values are "resurfaced once, just... only resurfaced once", and the comparison to `if st.button("1") and st.button("2")`, is exactly right. `_reset_triggers()` in `runtime/state/session_state.py` nulls every trigger value at the end of each run. With stable `data` a component mounts once and sends once, so after that value is consumed there is nothing left to re-send — two sequential mount-time triggers deadlock. Measured: the second component received a value **0 times across 126 runs**.

### Three corrections to this thread

1. **Trigger values do not require an `on_<key>_change` callback.** Earlier in the thread we said the key wouldn't appear in the result without one; that isn't right. None of our repros registered a callback and values arrived normally — the pushback on that point was correct.
2. **The `st.stop()` approach doesn't work.** It loops forever exactly like `st.rerun()` — the second component still never resolves. Worth stating plainly since it was suggested here and looked promising.
3. **The automated triage comment above is only half right.** Async module loading does explain an empty result on the *first* run, but it predicts convergence on run 2 — which is what a stable-`data` component actually does. It doesn't explain the permanent failure.

### What works reliably

| Pattern | Result |
|---|---|
| `setStateValue` with a stable key | resolves in **2 runs** |
| Five `setStateValue` components at once | all resolve together in **2 runs** |
| `setStateValue` on mount, changing `data` | 21/21 delivered |
| `setTriggerValue` from an event handler | 40/40 delivered |
| Inside `@st.fragment` | works |
| Inside an `if st.button(...)` block | never resolves — matching the second report above |

### The one genuine bug

Separately from the above: `setTriggerValue` called **during mount** loses roughly a quarter of values when the component remounts on changed `data`, even with an explicit `key` and a verified-stable element id. Filed as #16732. Both alternatives above are unaffected, so the practical guidance is unchanged — use `setStateValue` for initialization values.

### What we're doing with this issue

Since the reported "result dropping" turns out to be documented behaviour plus the separately-filed bug, we're converting this issue to the enhancement underneath it — a supported way to await an initialization value without leaving permanent `session_state` entries — which is what's actually being asked for here.

@JWCS @gRodrigues03 — this is the part we'd need your input on to design it. At the point of the call, what needs to be guaranteed: that the value is *present*, or just a reliable way to distinguish "not ready yet" from "genuinely empty"? And what makes a persistent `session_state` entry unacceptable — the volume, the staleness, or key hygiene? The point that "supply a default" can't distinguish an expected value from cache invalidation is the crux, and knowing which of those matters would shape the answer.

This is a real frontend bug, not a failed chart render. `st.altair_chart` (and the shared Vega-Lite path used by `st.vega_lite_chart` and builtin charts) strips datasets from the spec and sends them separately as Arrow. `useVegaEmbed.createView` then calls `vega-embed`'s `embed()`, which immediately runs the view, and only afterwards inserts Arrow data and calls `runAsync()` again. Vega therefore computes scale domains from empty data on that first run and logs `WARN Infinite extent for field "...": [Infinity, -Infinity]`. The chart still appears correctly after the second run; this is console noise on every render. A likely fix is to attach initial values to the spec before `embed()`, or to construct/run the Vega view only after datasets are inserted.

This is a cross-cutting API enhancement, not a bug: deprecate widget `on_change` / `on_click` `args`/`kwargs` in favor of `functools.partial`, and auto-pass the widget’s new value (and possibly key) into the callback as requested in #5305. Today those extra parameters exist on essentially every callback-capable widget; `register_widget` stores them on `WidgetMetadata`, and `SessionState.call_callback` invokes `callback(*args, **kwargs)` without injecting the widget value, so handlers still read `st.session_state`. That makes `args`/`kwargs` redundant with Python’s native partial application, while reusable callbacks stay awkward. This is not a duplicate of #5305 — it is a broader public-API cleanup that incorporates that request. It needs a spec, a backwards-compatible injection mechanism (signature detection vs. a fixed kwarg), and a long deprecation window.

### Related Issues

- [#5305](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5305) — Pass state as a parameter to `on_change`. This issue explicitly incorporates that request; auto-passing the new value (and possibly key) is the second half of the proposed API change.
- [#5498](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5498) — Directly provide form submission data to the form-submit callback. Same friction: callbacks currently take extra args via `kwargs` or look up keys in `st.session_state` instead of receiving values automatically.

In case it's useful, here's my quick attempt at doing string replace with a stream.
```python
import streamlit as st
from openai import OpenAI, Stream

client = OpenAI()

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[dict(role="user", content="Show me a quick example of an integral")],
    stream=True,
)


def parse_stream(stream: Stream):
    last_text = ""
    for chunk in stream:
        text = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
        if text:
            # Sometimes delimiters like \( can be split over two chunks.
            # If the previous chunk ended in \, prepend that to this chunk
            if last_text.endswith("\\"):
                text = last_text + text

            text = (
                text.replace(r"\[", "$$")
                .replace(r"\]", "$$")
                .replace(r"\(", "$")
                .replace(r"\)", "$")
            )
            last_text = text

            # If the text ends in \, we don't return it, we'll get include it in the next chunk
            if not text.endswith("\\"):
                yield text


st.write_stream(parse_stream(stream))
```

```python
    selectable_dates=selectable_dates
)
```

I've been working on an implementation for this that goes a step further — instead of just a boolean toggle, it adds a `quick_select_options` parameter that supports three modes:

- `None` (default) — current auto-enable behavior, no breaking change
- `{}` (empty dict) — explicitly disables quick select (addresses this issue)
- `{"Label": (start, end), ...}` — custom preset date ranges

```python
# Disable quick select
st.date_input("Pick dates", value=[], quick_select_options={})

# Custom presets
st.date_input(
    "Reporting period",
    value=[],
    min_value=date(2025, 1, 1),
    max_value=date.today() - timedelta(days=1),
    quick_select_options={
        "January": (date(2025, 1, 1), date(2025, 1, 31)),
        "Q1": (date(2025, 1, 1), date(2025, 3, 31)),
        "Year to date": (date(2025, 1, 1), timedelta(days=-1)),
        "Last 30 days": (timedelta(days=-30), timedelta(days=-1)),
    },
)
```

@lukasmasuch I think fixing this properly would require refactoring some non-test functionality as well. Specifically, right now all caches created within a single streamlit process are stored in two singletons: [_data_caches](https://github.com/Asaurus1/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_data_api.py#L309) and [_resource_caches](https://github.com/Asaurus1/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_data_api.py#L309). To allow different AppTest instances to have different cache storage we would need to either

* Move the responsibility of [storing caches between script runs](https://github.com/Asaurus1/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_data_api.py#L217) from the singleton `DataCaches`/`ResourceCaches` to the [`CacheStorageManager`](https://github.com/Asaurus1/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_data_api.py#L272) class (which currently is only used to create `Cache` instances, not retain them between runs. This would allow `AppTest` to inject a special `MemoryCacheStorageManager` which would be unique per `AppTest` instance.
* Make the `DataCaches`/`ResourceCaches` singletons not module-level singletons, and instead them live in the streamlit runtime instance. Then `AppTest` could create separate instances of them per `AppTest` instance.

I recently encountered a persistent Protobuf conflict when using Streamlit and Supervisely in the same Python project.
The issue appears as:

`TypeError: Conflict register for file "worker_api.proto": Empty is already defined in file "streamlit/proto/Empty.proto".
`

This occurs because both Streamlit and Supervisely define a top-level Protobuf message named 'Empty' without using package namespaces. When both libraries are imported into the same process, the global Protobuf descriptor pool registers two different 'Empty' messages with the same name, which raises a TypeError immediately.

The import order does not solve the problem since Streamlit Run loads Streamlit's internal modules (and its Empty.proto) before any user code is executed. Using multiprocessing with the 'spawn' start method does not help either, since the child process re-imports the main module, bringing Streamlit back into memory before Supervisely is imported and reproducing the same conflict.

The only reliable workaround I found is to isolate Supervisely in a separate process that never imports Streamlit.
In practice, this means delegating all Supervisely-related operations to a small subprocess (or CLI script) that communicates with the main Streamlit app via JSON over stdin/stdout. Each process then maintains its own independent Protobuf registry, completely avoiding the name collision.

This is a product-spec enhancement to add a first-class `st.column_config.DurationColumn` for `datetime.timedelta` / `pandas.Timedelta` / Arrow duration values. Elapsed time (negatives, multi-day, unwrapped hours) is a different type from `TimeColumn` (clock-of-day) and from `NumberColumn` (raw seconds with printf formats). There is no `DurationColumn` today: `column_config.py` and the frontend `ColumnTypes` map only expose date/time/number types, while the backend already classifies duration as `ColumnDataKind.TIMEDELTA` and treats `NumberColumn` as the only editing-compatible type. `st.data_editor` currently leaves timedelta columns uneditable by default to avoid JS integer overflow. The proposed type would own duration formats (`humanize`, elapsed `HH:mm:ss`), timedelta-typed `min`/`max`/`step`, and a real duration editor, while keeping `TimeColumn` clock-only.

### Related Issues

- [#9751](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9751) — `TimeColumn` on `pd.Timedelta` shows a wrong clock time (e.g. `1s` as `00:16:40`). This issue argues `TimeColumn` should reject durations and that elapsed-clock display belongs on `DurationColumn`.
- [#8949](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8949) — Timedelta columns sort by humanized strings (`14 days`, `2 hours`) instead of the underlying value. Mapping duration to `NumberColumn` (seconds) is the current workaround; `DurationColumn` would own numeric sort plus a duration-specific format/editor API.
- [#14557](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14557) — `column_config` silently ignores type mismatches. Same class of problem as applying `TimeColumn` to timedeltas; this issue asks for an error instead of a wrong clock time when the type cannot represent the value.

I looked into fixing this and want to record what I found, because I think the behavior follows from the fragment execution model rather than from a defect in the `st.rerun` plumbing — and because the obvious test harness cannot exercise it.

**`AppTest` cannot reproduce it.** I built the reported flow with a body-execution counter:

```python
@st.dialog("Expensive operation")
def my_dialog():
    st.session_state.body_runs += 1
    if st.button("Close", key="inner"):
        st.rerun()

if st.button("Open", key="outer"):
    my_dialog()
```

Driving it with `AppTest`: `body_runs` goes 0 → 1 when the dialog opens, and clicking the inner button gives **delta = 0** with the dialog closed (0 dialog blocks remaining). That is the *expected* behavior, not the bug.

The reason is that `AppTest.run()` only performs full script runs and never drives a **fragment-scoped** rerun. In `lib/streamlit/testing/v1/local_script_runner.py`, `fragment_ids_this_run` is forwarded only when the runner itself emits it; clicking a widget inside a fragment via `AppTest` does not take the fragment-rerun path the real frontend uses. So the failing path is unreachable from `AppTest`, and any unit test written there would pass vacuously.

**Why the plumbing looks correct.** Tracing the pieces:

- `elements/dialog_decorator.py` wraps the dialog body in `_fragment(...)` — a dialog *is* a fragment, and its own comment documents that closing requires `st.rerun()`.
- `commands/execution_control.py` → `_new_fragment_id_queue(ctx, "app")` returns `[]`, correctly clearing the queue so the next run is a full app run.
- `runtime/fragment.py` explicitly re-raises `RerunException` / `StopException`, so the fragment wrapper is not swallowing the rerun.

**So the mechanism appears inherent.** Any widget interaction inside a fragment re-runs that fragment. In the repro the expensive work sits *before* the button, so evaluating `if pressed:` necessarily re-executes it — before `st.rerun()` is ever reached. The dialog then closes correctly on the following app run. That ordering is a direct consequence of "widget interaction re-runs its fragment", which is also why the `st.session_state` sentinel + early-exit workaround suggested above works, and why an `on_click` callback avoids it (callbacks run before the script body).

**Which makes this a design question, not a bug fix.** Genuinely changing it would mean altering fragment rerun semantics for dialogs — e.g. suppressing the fragment rerun when the interaction will immediately request an app-scoped rerun, which is not knowable before the body runs. I did not want to guess at that in shared control-flow code, so I have not opened a PR.

If maintainers decide on a direction, two things are worth settling first:

1. Whether the intended contract is "a dialog body must be re-entrant across widget interactions" (in which case this is documentation) or "a dialog closing via `st.rerun()` should not re-execute its body" (in which case it is a semantics change).
2. If the latter, `AppTest` would need the ability to drive fragment-scoped reruns, otherwise the fix cannot be regression-tested at the unit level and would need e2e coverage.

Following up on my analysis above with an actual browser reproduction, because I got something wrong in the meantime and the diagnosis turns out to be sharper than I described.

**First, a correction.** In my comment above I said the obvious test harness cannot exercise this, which is true, but I then went on to state on PR #16287 that the bug "does not reproduce on current `develop`." That was wrong, and I've retracted it there. `AppTest` cannot drive a fragment-scoped rerun, so it structurally cannot observe this — that's a limitation of the harness, not evidence the behaviour is gone.


```
AFTER DONE:  'outside body runs: 2'
```

The body executes **twice**, confirming @MattRCole's report.

**`st.rerun()` is not the cause.** This is the part I think is worth recording. I removed the `st.rerun()` call entirely — leaving `if st.button("Done"): pass` — and re-ran:

```
AFTER OPEN:  'body runs: 1'
AFTER CLICK: 'body runs: 2'    # dialog still open, st.rerun() absent
```

Still twice. The second execution is caused purely by the widget interaction triggering a fragment-scoped rerun of the dialog body (a dialog *is* a fragment, via `_fragment(...)` in `elements/dialog_decorator.py`). `st.rerun()` only determines what happens *after* that second execution — it closes the dialog. It plays no part in the re-execution itself.

So the issue title is slightly misleading: this is not specific to `st.rerun` in a button conditional. Any widget interaction inside a dialog re-executes everything above that widget. `st.rerun()` just makes it conspicuous, because the user's mental model is "closing" rather than "re-running".

**Why the pre-button work cannot be skipped.** The button's return value is only observable by executing the body up to it. Deciding to skip the fragment rerun would require knowing in advance that the body is going to request an app-scoped rerun, which is not knowable before running it. That's the same conclusion as my earlier comment, now with the cause correctly isolated.

**Coverage gap.** I also claimed on the PR that `e2e_playwright/st_dialog_test.py:656` already covered this. It does not. That test uses `dialog_with_rerun` (`st_dialog.py:276`), where the button is the *first* statement in the body, with no preceding work and no counter — so it verifies the dialog **closes** across fragment and full-app reruns, not that the body doesn't re-execute. This behaviour is genuinely untested.

**Where that leaves the decision**, unchanged in shape but now better evidenced:

1. If the intended contract is "a fragment body re-executes on any widget interaction, dialogs included," this is documentation — and the guidance is the `st.session_state` sentinel + early exit that @MattRCole is already using, or `on_click` (callbacks run before the script body). Worth saying explicitly in the `st.dialog` docs, since the failure mode is silent and expensive.
2. If the intended contract is "a dialog body should execute once per user-visible interaction," that is a semantics change to fragment reruns, and the opt-in `frozen`-style parameter from the original request is probably the least invasive shape.

I have a Playwright probe (`probe_13009.py` + counter assertions) that pins the current 2× behaviour and would serve as the regression test for either direction. Happy to send it as a PR — as a test documenting intended behaviour under option 1, or as the failing test under option 2. Just let me know which contract you want.

To be clear about scope: I am not proposing a fix here, because both options are product decisions in shared control-flow code.

This issue reports a `NoSessionContext` error and "missing ScriptRunContext" warning when using Streamlit's `StreamlitCallbackHandler` with LangChain/LangGraph agents. The root cause is that when LangChain executes tools in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` worker thread (e.g., `ThreadPoolExecutor-4_0`), the thread lacks the Streamlit `ScriptRunContext` which is stored as a thread-local attribute. Without this context, Streamlit cannot enqueue UI update messages. The `StreamlitCallbackHandler` at `lib/streamlit/external/langchain/streamlit_callback_handler.py` calls Streamlit methods like `_container.update()` and `_container.markdown()` from callback functions, which internally require the `ScriptRunContext` to function properly.

**Potential fixes could include:**
1. Having `StreamlitCallbackHandler` capture and propagate the context to callback-executing threads
2. Documenting a pattern for users to manually propagate context using `add_script_run_ctx`
3. Improving multi-threading support in Streamlit's runtime

### Related Issues

- **#1326** - [Improve "missing ScriptRunContext" threading error](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/1326): This is the foundational issue for the same class of problems. It requests better error messaging and documentation for the "missing context" warning when using threads, and discusses the `add_report_ctx` (now `add_script_run_ctx`) workaround.

- **#7851** - [Make Streamlit more friendly to multi-threading](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7851): A general request to improve multi-threading support. Using threads with Streamlit currently requires manual context management with `add_script_run_ctx`, which is error-prone and not well-documented.

- **#8490** - [Add support for multi-threading/multi-processing in Streamlit](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8490): Request for native multi-threading support so users can run background tasks without blocking the main thread and without manually managing script contexts.

@mhollander Thanks for reporting this issue! I was able to reproduce it [here](https://issues.streamlit.app/?issue=gh-8934).

### Issue Analysis

This is a **bug** in `st.popover` positioning. When a popover contains many items, it is rendered *above* the trigger button on smaller viewports (e.g. a laptop/tablet screen, or when zoomed to ~150%) instead of below it. The reporter expects the popover to always open below the button and gain scrollbars if it is too tall for the available space.

**Likely root cause:** The popover body is positioned with Floating UI using a default `placement: "bottom-start"` plus the `flip()` middleware (see `frontend/lib/src/components/elements/Popover/Popover.tsx` and `frontend/lib/src/hooks/useFloatingOverlay.ts`). When there isn't enough room below the trigger, `flip()` intentionally repositions the popover above the trigger. There is currently no `size` middleware constraining the popover body's `max-height` to the available viewport space, so instead of clamping the height and enabling internal scrolling, the overlay flips upward. A fix would likely involve adding a `size` middleware to cap `max-height` (with `overflow-y: auto`) and/or tuning the flip/shift behavior so the popover stays anchored below the button. (Note: the popover was migrated from BaseWeb to Floating UI since this issue was filed in v1.35, but the flip-vs-clamp behavior still applies.)

### Related Issues

- [#9387 – Popover in sidebar is outside of the viewable page](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9387): Confirmed bug about popover positioning/overflow in the sidebar (same container context as this repro); both stem from viewport-aware repositioning not keeping the popover fully visible.
- [#10239 – Dynamic popover height](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10239): Requests the popover resize/scroll to fit content rather than being cut off — directly related to this issue's expected behavior of adding scrollbars instead of flipping.
- [#12046 – Allow selection of `st.popover` body placement](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12046): Enhancement to control the popover's opening direction, which overlaps with the placement/flip behavior causing this bug.
