One potential workaround here is to configure the columns to use `NumberColumn`:

```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(dict(timedelta=[pd.Timedelta(hours=2),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=1),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=3),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=14)]))

st.dataframe(df, column_config={"timedelta": st.column_config.NumberColumn()})
```

This is a confirmed bug where sorting timedelta columns in `st.dataframe` (and `st.data_editor`) uses the human-readable string representation ("14 days", "2 hours", "a day") rather than the underlying numeric value. The sorting is performed alphabetically on the formatted display strings, leading to incorrect sort order.

**Root Cause Analysis:** Timedelta/duration columns are handled by `NumberColumn` which uses `sortMode: "smart"`. When rendering, the column uses `formatArrowCell()` to produce human-readable strings via `moment.duration().humanize()`. The upstream `@glideapps/glide-data-grid-source` library's sorting appears to sort on the formatted display value rather than the raw numeric `data` field in the cell, even in "smart" mode. This is an upstream issue with the glide-data-grid library.

This is a frontend bug in the `st.date_input` calendar header: when `min_value`/`max_value` span a year boundary and the max date’s month/day is earlier than the min date’s (here `2024-08-03` → `2025-02-03`), the popover grid is on February 2025 but the header shows **February 2024**, and the year dropdown lists only **2024**. Selecting a day still commits the correct 2025 date, so the value path is fine; only the month/year picker UI is wrong. The same header is shared with `st.datetime_input`.

Likely cause: React Aria’s `CalendarYearPicker` (`useCalendarYearPicker`, `react-aria-components` 1.20.0) builds year options by starting at `minValue` and adding one year at a time until the date exceeds `maxValue`. `2024-08-03 + 1 year` is `2025-08-03`, which is after `2025-02-03`, so 2025 is never added. Streamlit then renders the year trigger from that item list (`CalendarPopoverHeader`), so it stays on the only remaining year (2024) even while the calendar grid shows February 2025. There is already a local workaround in `CalendarPopoverHeader` for a related RAC year-picker bug (stale month on controlled `focusedValue`), but it does not fix year-list generation. A secondary Streamlit issue: `getInitialFocusedDate` clamps to `minDate` but not `maxDate`, so with `value=None` and today after the max, the focused date starts out of range.

Branch: https://github.com/rajarshidattapy/streamlit/tree/fix/mem-address-regex-uppercase-hex

The library change is one character class:

```diff
+# CPython renders the address with the platform C runtime's pointer format, which
+# is lowercase hex on glibc but uppercase hex on Windows, so accept both.
 _OBJ_MEM_ADDRESS: Final = re.compile(
-    r"^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-f]+\>$"
+    r"^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-fA-F]+\>$"
 )
```

Plus two tests in `lib/tests/streamlit/string_util_test.py`: a parameterized case covering both hex casings and three non-address strings, and one that asserts against a repr produced by the running interpreter, so the behavior stays pinned on whichever platform CI runs.

Verification on Windows (Python 3.13.6, `develop` @ `2ac0d77d3`):

- The five existing tests named in the issue now pass: `write_test.py::test_obj_instance`, `::test_repr_html`, `::test_repr_html_no_html_tags_in_string`, `::test_repr_html_not_callable`, and `elements/help_test.py::StHelpTest::test_class_members`.

The `_OBJ_MEM_ADDRESS` regex uses `[0-9a-f]+`, so it fails on CPython's uppercase `%p` addresses (e.g. `0x0000027B0C1B1550`). `st.write()` then treats a default object `str()` as markdown instead of routing to the help view, and `st.help()` shows memory addresses as member values (dropping property docstrings). This is a real typing bug in `st.selectbox`, not a pyrefly-only issue. Overloads distinguish `index: int` vs `index: None` and `accept_new_options: Literal[False]` vs `Literal[True]`, then fall through to a catch-all of `index: int | None` + `accept_new_options: bool` that returns `T | str | None`. When `index` is typed as `int | None` (and `accept_new_options` is omitted / `False`), pyrefly/pyright cannot match the narrower overloads and pick that catch-all, so `str` appears in the return type even though a new option cannot be entered. mypy often expands the `index` union across overloads and reports `T | None`, which is why it stays silent. Existing type tests only cover literal `index=None` / `index=0`. A fix is to add an overload for `index: int | None` with `accept_new_options: Literal[False]` returning `T | None` (before the catch-all) and cover it in `lib/tests/streamlit/typing/selectbox_types.py`.

This is a real guest-to-host delivery bug in `HostCommunicationManager.sendMessageToHost`: it only `postMessage`s to `window.parent`. In the in-iframe embed topology (host preamble in the app frame; `window.parent` is a third-party page), that means the host never sees guest messages. `GUEST_READY` is the only exception — `openHostCommunication` also posts it to the app’s own window — which is why readiness works while `METRICS_EVENT` (`viewReport` / `updateReport` / `pageProfile`) and every other guest-to-host type are dropped. `MetricsManager` is not at fault: with `metricsUrl === "postMessage"` it correctly calls `sendMessageToHost`. The host-to-guest path already trusts same-window self-posts (`receiveHostMessage`), so the gap is one-directional. A same-window echo of all guest-to-host messages is a reasonable fix, but it must be tagged (e.g. `isGuestToHostEcho`) because `UPDATE_HASH` exists in both directions and would otherwise be executed as a host command if the app origin is allow-listed. `sendMessageToSameOriginHost` has the same parent-only limitation (used for `REDIRECT_TO_URL`).

### Related Issues

- [PR #14790](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14790) — added the same-window `GUEST_READY` dispatch this issue wants generalized to all guest-to-host messages.
- [PR #16327](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16327) — the host-to-guest counterpart: trusts same-window self-posts so an in-iframe preamble can deliver `SET_AUTH_TOKEN` when the parent is untrusted.
- [PR #15800](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/15800) — the source/`isTrusted` guard that made untagged self-posts unsafe; any echo of guest-to-host traffic has to be ignored by `receiveHostMessage`.

Long unbreakable markdown (file paths in list items) overflows the bordered `st.expander` when it is placed in `st.sidebar`. This looks like a CSS min-content issue rather than an expander animation bug: markdown uses `overflow-wrap: break-word` (and `word-break: break-word` only on `p`, not `li`), which does not shrink a flex item’s min-content width, while the expander details panel is `overflow: visible` with no `min-width: 0`. Nested flex layout (sidebar → expander → block) then lets long tokens paint past the expander border. A likely fix is `overflow-wrap: anywhere` / `word-break` on list content plus containing overflow on the expander panel. `#12366` addressed the same wrapping class in bordered containers and shipped in 1.49, but this 1.52 sidebar+expander case still reproduces.

**Related issues:**
- https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12366 — Same long-token markdown overflow in a bordered container; closed by adding `overflow-wrap: break-word`, which appears insufficient inside the sidebar expander flex layout.
- https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6394 — Long markdown (inline code) overflowing nested alert containers; same wrapping failure mode in a constrained parent.
- https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9387 — Nested content overflowing the sidebar viewport (`st.popover`); related sidebar overflow, different mechanism (positioning vs. text wrapping).

**Note**: This is a markdown list sizing regression rather than an `st.expander` or sidebar bug. 
Top-level lists carry `width: fit-content`, which is floored at `min-content`, and the `overflow-wrap: break-word` above it does not reduce `min-content` width — so a list holding an item too long to fit is sized to that item and never wraps. Paragraphs have `width: auto` and are unaffected, which is why the prose wraps and only the bullets spill. Introduced by #13036 (`text_alignment`) and shipped in 1.52.0.
**Impacted**: any container narrower than the longest list item. The sidebar clips the overflow, so the text is lost rather than just misaligned. 
**Not impacted**: full-width lists, lists whose items fit, nested lists, and widget labels.

## Update

Streamlit 1.61 will support a `refresh_mode="background"` for `cache_data` and `cache_resource` which allows expired values (based on `ttl`) to be updated in the background without blocking the user session.

It is also already possible to pre-warm caches at startup before the first user connects via `st.App` lifespan:

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from streamlit.starlette import App

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    print("🚀 Pre-caching data...")

    # Call cached functions to populate cache
    from myapp import load_data, compute_stats
    load_data("users")      # @st.cache_data
    load_data("products")   # @st.cache_data
    compute_stats()         # @st.cache_resource

    print("✅ Cache warmed!")
    yield
    
    # Run any close operations here

app = App("main.py", lifespan=lifespan)
```

The lifespan runs before the server accepts connections, so the first user gets instant cached results.

We are also planning to add a background job utility (+ cron scheduling) that would allow additional advanced ways to refresh caches in the background. This is tracked here: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6687

So I wrote a quick and dirty script that uses the internal websocket to mimic a user interaction, using only streamlit dependencies. This is still an ugly workaround/hack, but better than selenium I think.

````python
import argparse
import asyncio
import datetime

import tornado.websocket
from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToDict
from streamlit.proto.BackMsg_pb2 import BackMsg
from streamlit.proto.ClientState_pb2 import ClientState
from streamlit.proto.ForwardMsg_pb2 import ForwardMsg
from streamlit.proto.WidgetStates_pb2 import WidgetStates


class WebSocketClient:
    """client heavily inspired by https://gist.github.com/sadernalwis/0a110d280b090e751a8de50d97862a35"""

    def __init__(self, event_loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop, url):
        self.url = url
        self.connection: tornado.websocket.WebSocketClientConnection | None = None
        self.event_loop = event_loop
        self.last_message_date = None

    async def start(self):
        await self.connect_and_read()
        if self.connection is not None:
            self.connection.write_message(
                BackMsg(rerun_script=ClientState(widget_states=WidgetStates())).SerializeToString(),
                binary=True,
            )

    def stop(self):
        self.event_loop.stop()

    async def connect_and_read(self):
        print("Connecting to websocket...")
        await tornado.websocket.websocket_connect(
            url=self.url,
            callback=self.maybe_retry_connection,
            on_message_callback=self.on_message,
            ping_interval=10,
            ping_timeout=30,
        )

    def maybe_retry_connection(self, future) -> None:
        try:
            self.connection: tornado.websocket.WebSocketClientConnection | None = future.result()
        # would be better to check the exception type here and retry only if it's retryable
        # also add some sort of limit on retry
        except:
            print("Could not reconnect, retrying in 3 seconds...")
            self.event_loop.call_later(3, self.connect_and_read)

    def on_message(self, message):
        # weirdly seems to happen when closing the websocket, didn't check why
        if not message:
            return

        # not useful in my example, but we could add another coroutine that check every second if the self.last_message is too old and create some sort of timeout,
        # or for very long script you could need to send an heartbeat using BackMsg(app_heartbeat=True)
        self.last_message_date = datetime.datetime.now()

        # retrieving and parsing the websocket message
        f_message = ForwardMsg()
        f_message.ParseFromString(message)
        message_dict = MessageToDict(f_message)

        # we detect that the script is finished
        if message_dict.get("scriptFinished"):
            print(message_dict.get("scriptFinished"))
            # we could also send a rerun BackMsg with different widget state or another page to run another streamlit script
            # else we just stop the websocket client
            self.stop()


def get_arg_parser() -> argparse.Namespace:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument(
        "--url",
        type=str,
        default="ws://localhost:8501/_stcore/stream",
        help="url of the target streamlit instance",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()
    return args


def main():
    args = get_arg_parser()
    event_loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    client = WebSocketClient(event_loop, args.url)
    asyncio.ensure_future(client.start())
    event_loop.run_forever()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

````

Thanks for working on this. If I understand the spec correctly, this will essentially extend the caching to 2 x TTL, where a background refresh will get triggered between 1x <-> 2x TTL.  Beyond 2x TTL it's existing blocking cache refresh behavior.

So this will solve some subset of use cases, but will not help for infrequently accessed slow functions (where typical time between usage is longer than the tolerable data staleness/TTL).

The PR and spec discuss the potential unbound memory/resource problem that comes with solutions that would proactively refresh the cache before TTL expiration (unbound combinations of cached function parameters).  And some complexity of needing a background scheduler thread of some sort. However, it would be good for a future implementation to include this, with the user making the choice knowingly (and potentially with a max entry upper bound).

I sometime use the pattern where my cached slow function is only ever executed with one set of parameters, returning potentially more data to some calling function than necessary, and let that calling function do further filtering.  This calling function is not cached and has the  unbound arbitrary user supplied parameters.  This was I get more cache hits at the expense of a bit more filtering compute.

That pattern would benefit greatly from an "eager"/"proactive" cache refresher that executes before TTL expiration.

@ee-github thanks, great feedback! We have been thinking about this aspect quite a bit when designing the background refresh mode. The current solution is a bit of a balance to have a simple API with minimal risk for users of blowing up memory and compute. 

But the good news is that it is already possible to implement a scheduled background refresh via `lifespan` in `st.App`, e.g.:

```python
# data.py
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_data(ttl="1h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data(dataset: str):
    return fetch_expensive_data(dataset)
```

```python
# app.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
import logging

import anyio
import streamlit as st

from data import load_data

_LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)


async def keep_cache_warm() -> None:
    while True:
        try:
            # Cheap while fresh. Once stale, this returns the stale value and
            # triggers Streamlit's deduplicated background refresh.
            await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(load_data, "dashboard")
        except Exception:
            _LOGGER.exception("Scheduled cache refresh failed")

        await anyio.sleep(60)  # Check freshness every minute


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_app: st.App) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    async with anyio.create_task_group() as task_group:
        task_group.start_soon(keep_cache_warm)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            task_group.cancel_scope.cancel()


app = st.App("dashboard.py", lifespan=lifespan)
```

And we are planning to make this even simpler with a native utility command to define background tasks (related request: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6687).

This is a **feature request / enhancement** for `st.multiselect`. When many options are selected, the chips wrap onto multiple lines, causing the widget to grow vertically and break compact layouts or misalign with adjacent widgets (e.g. `st.selectbox`, `st.button`). The request is to add a way to keep the widget's height fixed, e.g. a `wrap=False` parameter that keeps selected chips on a single (scrollable) line, and/or to summarize selections in the dropdown. Since this is a widget-styling/layout behavior with a small, well-scoped surface, the existing `type:enhancement`, `feature:st.multiselect`, `area:layout`, and `papercut` labels fit well. This is part of a broader family of "control wrap behavior" requests the author has filed across widgets and containers.

### Related Issues

- [#13516 — Option to not wrap `st.segmented_control` while displaying on a page](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13516): The closest analog — another chip/tag-based widget where the request is an option to prevent items from wrapping. This is a bug in the OIDC logout flow when using AWS Cognito as the identity provider. The root cause is in `build_logout_url()` in [`lib/streamlit/auth_util.py`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/auth_util.py#L223-L226), which constructs the logout URL using the standard OIDC RP-Initiated Logout parameter name `post_logout_redirect_uri`. However, AWS Cognito's logout endpoint does **not** follow the OIDC RP-Initiated Logout specification — it expects the parameter to be named `redirect_uri` (or `logout_uri`) instead. When Streamlit sends `post_logout_redirect_uri`, Cognito rejects it with "Required String parameter 'redirect_uri' is not present". The logout itself still succeeds server-side (cookies are cleared before the redirect), which is why pressing the browser back button shows the user as logged out.

A potential fix would be to either detect Cognito-style endpoints and use the appropriate parameter name, or to allow users to configure custom logout parameters for non-standard providers.

### Related Issues

- **#12144** ([st.logout() doesn't redirect to correct Cognito ESE](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12144)) — CLOSED. Very similar Cognito logout issue from v1.48.0 where `client_id` was missing from the logout URL. Fixed via revert in 1.48.1, but the underlying Cognito parameter naming incompatibility (`post_logout_redirect_uri` vs `redirect_uri`) was not addressed.
- **#12169** ([Breaking Change: Streamlit 1.48 breaks st.logout()](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12169)) — CLOSED. Related regression where `post_logout_redirect_uri` caused errors with Auth0 as well, confirming that multiple providers have non-standard logout parameter expectations.
- **#11703** ([Allow advanced customization of OIDC/OAuth2 parameters in st.login()](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11703)) — OPEN. Enhancement request for customizable OIDC parameters that could serve as a workaround for provider-specific logout parameter requirements.

## Reproduction Assessment: **CONFIRMED** (via code analysis)

This bug is confirmed real. I was unable to do a live reproduction (no Cognito user pool available), but the root cause is unambiguous from the source code.

### Root Cause

In [`lib/streamlit/auth_util.py:223-226`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/auth_util.py#L223-L226), `build_logout_url()` hardcodes the OIDC standard parameter name `post_logout_redirect_uri`:

```python
logout_params: dict[str, str] = {
    "client_id": client_id,
    "post_logout_redirect_uri": post_logout_redirect_uri,
}
```

AWS Cognito's logout endpoint does **not** follow the OIDC RP-Initiated Logout spec. It requires `redirect_uri` (or `logout_uri`), not `post_logout_redirect_uri`. It also ignores `id_token_hint`.

So Streamlit sends: `?client_id=...&post_logout_redirect_uri=...&id_token_hint=...`
But Cognito expects: `?client_id=...&redirect_uri=...`

This matches the exact error reported: *"Required String parameter 'redirect_uri' is not present"*

### Why logout still works

The server-side logout (cookie clearing) happens **before** the redirect to the provider's logout endpoint. So the Streamlit session is invalidated regardless of whether the provider redirect succeeds — which is why pressing back shows the user as logged out.

### Scope

This likely affects any OIDC provider whose `end_session_endpoint` doesn't follow the RP-Initiated Logout spec parameter naming. Related: #12169 showed Auth0 had the same issue.

A potential fix would be to allow users to configure custom logout query parameters, or to detect non-standard providers and adjust the parameter name accordingly.

Hey! The diagnosis here seems right. Cognito's logout endpoint doesn't follow the OIDC RP-Initiated Logout spec and expects `redirect_uri` instead of `post_logout_redirect_uri`.

I put together a draft PR (#14868) that adds an optional `[auth.logout_params]` section to secrets.toml so you can override the default parameter names. For Cognito it'd look like:

```toml
[auth.logout_params]
redirect_uri_name = "redirect_uri"
include_id_token_hint = false
```

@sfc-gh-bnisco @jrieke I like this feature idea. If you confirm below proposal, I'll start off with the implementation. 🚀 

### Scope
Add `bind="local-storage"` only for widgets that already support `bind="query-params"`.

### Behavior
- On mount: initialize from `localStorage` if a value exists and is valid.
- On change: write widget value to `localStorage`.
- If `localStorage` is unavailable or errors: silently fall back to normal widget behavior.
- If stored value is invalid/stale for current widget config: ignore it and attempt to delete that key.

### Name spacing
```
stWidgetBindLocalStorage-${enc(pageLinkBaseUrl)}-${enc(window.location.pathname)}-v${WIDGET_BIND_LOCAL_STORAGE_VERSION}-${enc(bindKey)}

```

`WIDGET_BIND_LOCAL_STORAGE_VERSION` is for schema evolution/migration safety.
```
const WIDGET_BIND_LOCAL_STORAGE_VERSION = 1
```

Keep `key` optional, but recommend explicit `key` for durable persistence across app changes.

#### Collision handling:
- Cross-app: `pageLinkBaseUrl`
- Cross-page: `pathname`
- Per-widget: `bindKey`

### Clear Policy
- On `st.logout()`, clear all `bind="local-storage"` entries for the current app namespace only.
- Pruning-on-default: when a bound widget returns to default, remove that widget’s localStorage key.

#### Programmatic
New API:

```python
BindStorageTarget: TypeAlias = Literal["local-storage"]

def clear_bound_storage(*, bind: BindStorageTarget) -> None:
```

- `st.clear_bound_storage(bind="local-storage")` clears current app namespace only.
- `BindStorageTarget` can be extended later (e.g. `"session-storage"`), if needed.

### Size/Limits
- No strict item-size caps yet.
- Handle `setItem` failures (`QuotaExceededError` / `SecurityError`) gracefully.
- Pruning-on-default will reduce storage pressure.

This is a **layout enhancement** request (not a bug). With the Flex layout, `width="stretch"` / `height="stretch"` make elements fill the remaining space, but when several siblings all use `"stretch"` they split the space equally with no way to weight them. The ask is to add a relative "weight" to stretch (e.g. `width="stretch:2"`, `width=("stretch", 2)`, or a `scale=N` parameter) so space is distributed proportionally among sibling stretch elements—mirroring `st.columns([2, 1])`. The exact API is still under discussion. Suggested labels: `type:enhancement`, `area:layout` (already applied by the team).

### Related Issues

- [#11715 — Make elements take up a relative amount of available width](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11715): Explicitly referenced here; both want to express width relative to available space rather than only fixed pixels or plain `stretch`. This issue's weighted-stretch proposal is one concrete way to satisfy that demand.
- [#12900 — Multiple elements with `width="stretch"` should have same width](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12900): Explicitly referenced here; it covers the default distribution behavior of multiple stretch siblings, while this issue adds the ability to make that distribution *unequal* via weights.
- [#12899 — Support `min_width` in flex containers](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12899): Closely related flex-layout sizing control; both aim to give developers finer control over how stretch/flex elements size themselves within a container.

Below is the code that helps to partially solve the problem with loading, through the spinner and a set of values from the local storage to the session state, then the local storage is accessed only once when the session state is empty.

Streamlit also has a problem with entering data in the fields https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/form-submit-works-only-on-odd-tries/29804
in this code a partial solution to this problem too

The solution is far from ideal, but at least slightly overlaps the problem. I hope this will be useful to you

```python
import time
import json
import streamlit as st
from streamlit_javascript import st_javascript


def get_from_local_storage(k):
    v = st_javascript(
        f"JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('{k}'));"
    )
    return v or {}


def set_to_local_storage(k, v):
    jdata = json.dumps(v)
    st_javascript(
        f"localStorage.setItem('{k}', JSON.stringify({jdata}));"
    )


TOOL_PREFIX = 'name_of_tool'
INPUT_FIELDS = ['first_input', 'second_input']

if st.session_state.get(TOOL_PREFIX):
    saved_result = st.session_state[TOOL_PREFIX]
else:
    with st.spinner():
        saved_result = get_from_local_storage(TOOL_PREFIX)
        # without sleep doesn't always load on time
        time.sleep(0.5)

# this for solving field problem 
# https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/form-submit-works-only-on-odd-tries/29804
for field in INPUT_FIELDS:
    if field not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state[field] = saved_result.get(field, '')


def save_update_state(st_data: dict):
    st.session_state[TOOL_PREFIX] = st_data
    set_to_local_storage(TOOL_PREFIX, st_data)


with st.form(key='test_form'):
    inp = st.text_input(label='Enter some data',
                        key='first_input')
    btn = st.form_submit_button('Go on!')
    if inp and btn:
        saved_result['first_input'] = inp
        st.success('Its ok')
        save_update_state(saved_result)
    elif btn:
        st.warning('Put something in text area')

with st.form(key='test_form_2'):
    inp = st.text_input(label='Enter some data',
                        key='second_input')
    btn = st.form_submit_button('Go on!')
    if inp and btn:
        saved_result['second_input'] = inp
        st.success('Its ok')
        save_update_state(saved_result)
    elif btn:
        st.warning('Put something in text area')

st.write(st.session_state)

```

Example:
```

from typing import TypedDict, cast

class MyClass:
    def __init__(self):
        self.foo = 'foo'
        self.bar = 42
    
    def get_foo(self) -> str:
        return self.foo
    
    def calculate_something(self, value: int) -> int:
        return self.bar * value

# Initialize the object in session state
if 'my_class' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['my_class'] = MyClass()

# Current behavior - no type hints available
# When typing: st.session_state['my_class'].
# The IDE does not provide suggestions for methods like get_foo() or calculate_something()

This issue reports `st.switch_page` navigating to a blank page instead of the target page, with the URL not updating. The same author previously reported this in #14709, which was closed as cannot-reproduce. This new issue includes full reproducible code.

**Root cause analysis:** The user's entrypoint (`project.py`) uses third-party components (`EncryptedCookieManager` from `streamlit_cookies_manager_ext` and `streamlit_js_eval`) that can call `st.stop()` or trigger `st.rerun()` **before** `st.navigation()` runs. Critically, the code checks `if "cookie_manager" not in st.session_state` but only ever sets `st.session_state["cookies"]` — so the key `"cookie_manager"` is never stored. This means a new `EncryptedCookieManager` is created on every rerun, and `cookies.ready()` likely returns `False` on the first render (since the component requires a browser round-trip), triggering `st.stop()` before `st.navigation()` executes. When `st.switch_page` triggers a rerun, `st.navigation()` never runs, so no navigation message is sent to the frontend, resulting in a blank page.

This appears to be a **user code issue** (session state key mismatch) rather than a Streamlit framework bug. However, it does highlight a usability concern: when `st.stop()` is called before `st.navigation()` during a page-switch rerun, the result is a silent blank page with no error feedback.

This is a **performance bug / regression follow-up** for `st.selectbox` with a very large option list (thousands+) when the widget is placed inside an `st.popover`. It is the residual case of #15863 (the ~16k-option freeze regression in 1.59.0), which was fixed for the standalone selectbox in 1.59.2 by virtualizing the dropdown option list (#15870). The reporter confirms the top-level case is fixed but says opening the popover and loading the options is still slow, and gets worse after opening/closing a few times.

**Likely root cause (needs confirmation):** The virtualization in `VirtualDropdown`/`Selectbox` only windows the *DOM rows* that are rendered, not the underlying React Aria `ComboBox` collection, so an internal node is still built for every option. On a top-level selectbox that O(n) build happens once at mount. `st.popover`, however, only mounts its body children while it is open (`{open && <FloatingPortal>…{children}…}` in `frontend/lib/src/components/elements/Popover/Popover.tsx`), so each reopen fully remounts the selectbox and re-runs the `selectOptions`/`displayOptions` mapping plus the full collection build for all ~10k options (`frontend/lib/src/components/shared/Dropdown/Selectbox.tsx`). Repeated open/close therefore repeats the expensive work each time, which matches the reported behavior. The popover's floating-positioning and outside-click/overlay handling add some extra per-open overhead on top of this.

### Related Issues

- **#15863** — [`st.selectbox` with many options (~16k) freezes on open in 1.59.0 (regression from 1.58.0)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15863): The parent regression this issue directly follows up on. Fixed for the general case in 1.59.2 (via #15870), but this issue reports the fix is incomplete inside `st.popover`.
- **#7104** — [Allow developer to limit the max number of results in the `st.selectbox` dropdown to improve widget performance](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7104): Long-standing request targeting the same underlying problem — rendering/handling thousands of options is expensive.
- **#7807** — [Typeahead/autocomplete (async) `st.selectbox` widget](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7807): Proposes async/server-side option loading, an alternative approach to avoid materializing very large option lists on the client.

While working in adjacent code I found a concrete, testable hypothesis for why this is specific to popovers. Sharing it rather than sitting on it — but flagging up front that **this is from code inspection, not profiling**, so it is a lead rather than a confirmed root cause.

## The asymmetry

`frontend/lib/src/components/shared/Dropdown/Selectbox.tsx` bounds Floating UI's `flip`/`shift` to the viewport, but **only** when the widget is in the sidebar:

```ts
const boundary = document.documentElement
return {
  ...base,
  flipOptions: { boundary },
  shiftOptions: { boundary, padding: SHIFT_VIEWPORT_PADDING },
}
```

Its own comment explains why:

> In the sidebar, flip/shift are bounded by the viewport (`document.documentElement`) rather than the sidebar's `overflow: auto` clipping rect. Otherwise the dropdown cannot flip up when the trigger sits near the bottom of the sidebar and it overflows the viewport instead (issue #16181).

`StyledPopoverBody` is the same shape of container:

```ts
maxHeight: "70vh",
overflow: "auto",
```

So a popover is also a scrollable clipping ancestor, but it gets no equivalent treatment — inside one, flip/shift resolve against the popover's small clipping rect instead of the viewport.

## Why that could show up as slowness rather than mispositioning

`autoUpdate` re-runs positioning on scroll and resize. With a cramped boundary, each pass has more work to reconcile, and the dropdown here is a virtualized list of 10k rows whose scroll container is itself inside the clipped popover. That combination is a plausible route from "wrong boundary" to "feels slow", and it would explain both why 1.59.2's virtualization fix didn't cover this case and why the symptom is popover-specific.

## What I have *not* established

I could not distinguish these two candidates by reading code, and they call for different fixes:

1. **Positioning thrash** — `autoUpdate` doing repeated work against the popover's clipping rect.
2. **Virtualizer mis-measurement** — the viewport height the RAC Virtualizer measures being wrong or unstable inside the popover, causing it to render far more rows than needed (which would partly defeat virtualization and match the "hangs above 10,000 options" description).

Both are consistent with the evidence above. Confirming which needs the repro in a browser with a profile of the open/close cycle, comparing in-popover against the same selectbox at top level.

I deliberately stopped short of a fix, because a boundary change to shared dropdown positioning touches every selectbox — and if the real cause is (2), a positioning change would look plausible while not moving the numbers at all.

If a maintainer wants to take this further, the two things worth measuring first are the count of `autoUpdate` position passes per popover open, and the number of `ListBoxItem` rows actually mounted, in-popover versus top-level.

This is a real cache-key collision in `@st.cache_data` / `@st.cache_resource`, not a hash-function accident. `_make_value_key` in `lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/cache_utils.py` folds each argument name and value into one hasher via sequential `update_hash` calls, and `hashing.py` encodes strings as `b"<type>:<payload>"` (e.g. `b"str:doc1"`) with no length prefix or field delimiter. Distinct calls such as `load("doc1", "acme")` and `load("doc1str:orgstr:acme")` therefore concatenate to the same byte string and share one value key, so the second call is a silent false hit. Defaulted arguments that were not passed are also omitted from the key, which makes this particular pair collide; the same delimiter-free `hasher.update` pattern is used for list/tuple items in `hashing.py`, so similar boundary collisions are possible there too. Length-prefixing (or otherwise delimiting) each field before hashing would make the key injective; that change would invalidate existing in-memory and `persist="disk"` entries once.

### Related Issues

- [#14622](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14622) — Closed. Confirmed `@st.cache_data` hash collisions that also produced silent false cache hits, via undersampling of large arrays/frames and omitted PIL palettes rather than argument-boundary concatenation. Same class of correctness/security failure (wrong cached value returned).
- [#11157](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11157) — Open. This is a valid bug in `st.slider`'s date/datetime path. Timelike values are serialized as microseconds since the epoch and sent as JavaScript numbers, which only preserve exact integers within `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (~±2^53, roughly 1684–2255). Int/float sliders already reject out-of-range bounds via `JSNumber.validate_*_bounds`, but the timelike branch is explicitly a no-op (`# No validation yet`), so moderately out-of-range dates are accepted and silently lose precision. Separately, default `min_value`/`max_value` are always computed as `value ± timedelta(days=14)` before checking whether the caller supplied bounds, which raises a bare `OverflowError` near `date.min`/`date.max` instead of a `StreamlitAPIException`. Fixing this should validate the microsecond form against JS safe-integer limits (not the incorrect 0001–9999 TODO range) and avoid computing unused default bounds that can overflow.

One more deployment shape that the shared slot affects, found while reviewing #16476.

A reverse proxy that forwards without `proxy_set_header Host $host` gives Streamlit a `Host` value such as `127.0.0.1:8501`, while the browser still sends the real page origin in `Origin`. Streamlit compares `Origin` against the `Host` header, so it treats that handshake as cross-origin even though the browser considers it same-origin.

A plain app still connects there, because its page can read the XSRF cookie and fill the token slot. An app that uses `useExternalAuthToken` cannot, because the host auth token occupies the slot the XSRF token needs. After #16476 that handshake is rejected with code `1008` rather than connecting anonymously.

Two ways to fix it, both inside the scope of this issue:

1. Carry the host auth token and the XSRF token in separate `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` entries, which fixes the identity gap and this rejection together.
2. Accept `browser.serverAddress` as an additional same-origin signal, so a proxy that hides the public host does not turn same-origin traffic into cross-origin traffic. That is operator-configured, so it does not trust `X-Forwarded-Host`.

Item by item.

**Item 2, WebSocket error messages. Confirmed bug.**

Malformed protobuf frames bypass the app-error redaction path. Because of this, `client.showErrorDetails` does not apply. File paths and line numbers can leak. This is a bug.

`client.showErrorDetails = "none"` still helps for application exceptions. It does not cover this path.

**Item 5, WebSocket Origin validation. Partly valid.**

`server.allowedHosts` was added in **1.61.0**. It validates the `Host` header on the WebSocket handshake. It still works when CORS is disabled. This helps with unexpected hostnames. It does not provide a strict `Origin` allow-list.

`server.corsAllowedOrigins` only adds more allowed origins. It does not replace the built-in allowed set. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0`, and the server's internal and external IPs are still allowed. `server.enableCORS=false` also allows all origins. This needs a separate feature request.

**Item 3, OS version disclosure. Partly overstated.**

Streamlit does not send a kernel version or distro version here. The `server_os` field is only `platform.system().lower()`. On Linux, this value is `"linux"`.

The same session message still exposes the full Streamlit version and full Python version to any client that can open the WebSocket. The Streamlit version is used for client auto-reload after a server upgrade. The Python version and OS name are used only for telemetry in the current frontend.

**Item 1, `Server` header. Resolved as written, but still present.**

On current releases, the header is `Server: uvicorn`. It is not `TornadoServer/6.x.x`. It does not include a version. Streamlit does not have a config option to remove it. The current workaround is to strip it at the proxy.

**Item 4, `/_stcore/host-config`. Informational.**

This endpoint returns mostly hardcoded open-source defaults and your configured `client.allowedOrigins`. It does not reveal deployment-specific secrets. For a non-embedded app, `client.allowedOrigins = []` is the correct setting.

Do not block this endpoint on the default connection path. If you need to control it, override the response at the proxy and return valid JSON.

## Reproduction Results — All Three Bugs Confirmed

I reproduced all three reported hash collisions against the current `develop` branch (`lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/hashing.py`).

### Bug 1a — NumPy sampling collision (seed=0)

Two arrays with 510,000 elements that differ only at non-sampled positions produce identical hashes:

```text
arr_a hash: 68322062a574164a6eba20f0626e5e32
arr_b hash: 68322062a574164a6eba20f0626e5e32
COLLISION: True
```

### Bug 1b — Pandas DataFrame sampling collision (random_state=0)

Two DataFrames with 55,000 rows that differ only at non-sampled rows produce identical hashes:

```text
df_a hash: 30563bf8063974ed7b4a40da2b62f0e3
df_b hash: 30563bf8063974ed7b4a40da2b62f0e3
COLLISION: True
```

### Bug 2 — PIL P-mode palette omission

Two P-mode images with identical pixel indices but different color palettes (black vs red) produce identical hashes:

```text
img_a hash: ae16f3aab7562c60cedc051dd3a40c61
img_b hash: ae16f3aab7562c60cedc051dd3a40c61
COLLISION: True
```

All reproductions used the exact scripts from the issue description. The bugs are real and straightforward to exploit.

Both halves of this report are now fixed, so closing.

This issue covered two distinct defects, which is why neither PR used a closing keyword — each only partially addressed it:

**1. PIL P-mode palette omission** — fixed in #15397 (merged 2026-06-04, `fec0f584da`). `tobytes()` returns only palette indices, not the colour table, so two P-mode images with identical indices and different palettes hashed the same. The palette is now included in the hash.

**2. Hash collision via the fixed sampling seed** — fixed in #16284 (merged just now, `a2414ead3f`), which adds the `runner.cacheHashSeed` config option.

On the second one, worth being precise about what it does and does not do. Large pandas/polars/numpy objects are still hashed from a sample rather than in full, because hashing them completely is substantially slower — measured at roughly 37–47x for a 10M-element numpy array. So the seed does not eliminate collisions; it **relocates** them. It is an escape hatch for an app that has actually hit a collision, letting you move which positions are sampled so the two colliding objects stop mapping to the same key.

If you need hashing to be exact rather than merely differently-sampled, the durable answer remains `hash_funcs`:

```python
@st.cache_data(hash_funcs={pd.DataFrame: lambda df: pd.util.hash_pandas_object(df).sum()})
def my_func(df): ...
```

That bypasses sampling entirely for the given type.

The option accepts an integer from 0 to 4294967295. The default is `0`, which is exactly the value that was hard-coded before, so existing cache keys are unchanged by the upgrade. Anything unusable — out of range, non-numeric, `true`, `inf` — is ignored with a logged warning and falls back to the default rather than raising from the hashing path.

Note that changing the seed invalidates every existing cache entry for large objects, so it should be kept stable across restarts and across replicas if you use a shared or persisted cache.

Confirmed regression in Streamlit 1.57.0 on FIPS-enforcing Python environments (e.g. RHEL 9 with FIPS mode, Chainguard `python-fips`). PR [#14842](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14842) replaced the previous MD5-based fast hasher with `hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=16)` in `create_fast_hasher` (`lib/streamlit/util.py:74`) but did not pass `usedforsecurity=False`. On a FIPS-restricted OpenSSL, `blake2b` is blocked by default and raises `ValueError: blake2b is blocked when usedforsecurity=True`, breaking every code path that uses `create_fast_hasher()` / `calc_hash()` — element ID generation, cache key computation, file-watcher hashing, fragment IDs, etc. The previous MD5 implementation correctly passed `usedforsecurity=False` (added in PR [#10413](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/10413) to fix [#10412](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10412)), so this is effectively a reintroduction of the same class of FIPS bug. The fix is a one-line change: `hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=16, usedforsecurity=False)` (and a regression test that exercises FIPS-style enforcement).

### Related Issues

- [#10412](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10412) — Streamlit fragment feature broke on a FIPS-compliant python image (same failure mode, fixed previously by adding `usedforsecurity=False` to MD5 calls).

- [#7526](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7526) — "Making streamlit FIPS compliant" — broader FIPS compliance tracking issue; this regression undoes part of that effort.

### Issue Analysis

This is a regression introduced in **Streamlit 1.57.0**, which switched the default web server from Tornado to **Starlette + Uvicorn** (#14553). The user is on **Windows + Python 3.12 + Streamlit 1.58**, using the new `st.App(...)` API.

The key symptom is that `http://127.0.0.1:8501` works, but `http://localhost:8501` hangs on the loading screen with the browser console reporting:

> WebSocket connection to 'ws://localhost:8501/_stcore/stream' failed: WebSocket is closed before the connection is established.

…and the server log shows `ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]` from `_ProactorBasePipeTransport` (Windows asyncio).

**Likely root cause: IPv4-only binding on Windows.**

- The default `server.address` is `"0.0.0.0"` (`DEFAULT_SERVER_ADDRESS` in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_server_config.py`).
- In `_bind_socket` (`lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_server.py`), an address without a `:` is bound as `socket.AF_INET` only — so the server listens exclusively on IPv4.
- On modern Windows, `localhost` is resolved to `::1` (IPv6) before `127.0.0.1` via `getaddrinfo` (and Chrome/Edge/Firefox honor that order). The browser therefore opens the WebSocket against `[::1]:8501`, which the IPv4-only socket isn't listening on, so Windows immediately resets the connection (WinError 10054) and the WS handshake never completes.
- The legacy Tornado server used `bind_sockets`, which iterates `getaddrinfo` results and binds separate sockets per family, so both `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` worked out of the box. The new Starlette path doesn't do dual-stack binding for `0.0.0.0`.

A likely workaround until this is fixed is to either (a) keep using `http://127.0.0.1:8501`, or (b) set `server.address = "::"` (or `"localhost"`) in `.streamlit/config.toml`, which goes through the IPv6/dual-stack code path that already sets `IPV6_V6ONLY=0`. The "corporate network / server" symptoms in the original report may be a separate issue (firewalls, reverse-proxy host headers, `client.allowedOrigins`) and would be worth verifying separately once the localhost case is resolved.

### Triage summary

This is a **dependency-compatibility bug** in Streamlit's web server, not a Community Cloud–specific problem — it affects any environment where a fresh install resolves Starlette to a newer release (Community Cloud just happens to auto-resolve the latest compatible versions).

**Root cause:** Streamlit's custom gzip middleware (`lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_gzip_middleware.py`) subclasses and directly instantiates Starlette's *internal* `GZipResponder`/`IdentityResponder` classes, which are private implementation details rather than public API:

```python
responder = _MediaAwareGZipResponder(
    self.app, self.minimum_size, compresslevel=self.compresslevel
)
```

`_MediaAwareGZipResponder` does not override `__init__`, so it inherits Starlette's constructor. A newer Starlette release changed `GZipResponder.__init__` to add a required keyword-only argument `thread_minimum_size`. Because the responder is instantiated without it, startup fails before any app code runs:

```
TypeError: GZipResponder.__init__() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'thread_minimum_size'
```

Streamlit's runtime dependency range in `lib/pyproject.toml` is `starlette>=0.46.0,<2`, so the incompatible Starlette version satisfies the upper bound (`<2`) and gets installed. This coupling to Starlette internals was introduced with the Starlette/Uvicorn server migration ([#14553](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14553)).

**Workaround confirmed by multiple reporters:** pin `starlette<1.4.0` (e.g. `starlette==1.3.1`) in `requirements.txt`.

**Suggested fix:** cap the Starlette upper bound below the breaking release (and/or make the middleware resilient to the changed responder signature, e.g. forward `thread_minimum_size` or stop relying on the private responder classes).

### Related Issues

- [#15378 – Running Streamlit with Starlette in Corporate Network](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15378): Another `area:server` bug stemming from the Starlette/Uvicorn migration; related to server behavior introduced by the same migration, though a different symptom (WebSocket connectivity).
- [#15022 – Intermittent `OSError: [WinError 121]` since upgrading to `v1.57.0`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15022): Also traces back to the 1.57 Starlette/Uvicorn migration and touches the same server layer, indicating shared risk in the new Starlette stack.

No existing issue appears to be a duplicate of this specific `GZipResponder`/Starlette-version incompatibility.

### Summary

This is a **regression on Windows** introduced by the Tornado → Starlette/Uvicorn server migration (v1.57). When the default port `8501` is already in use, Streamlit no longer auto-increments to the next free port; instead every process happily binds to `8501`.

**Likely root cause:** The new server pre-binds its own socket in `_bind_socket()` and unconditionally sets `SO_REUSEADDR`:

```271:271:lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_server.py
        sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
```

On POSIX systems `SO_REUSEADDR` only permits rebinding sockets left in `TIME_WAIT`, but **on Windows it allows two active sockets to bind the exact same address/port simultaneously**. As a result the second `streamlit run` process binds `8501` successfully, `bind()` never raises `EADDRINUSE`, and the port-retry loop in `UvicornServer.start()` (`for attempt in range(MAX_PORT_SEARCH_RETRIES + 1)`, ~lines 354–392) never advances to the next port. The old Tornado server relied on `tornado.netutil.bind_sockets`, which on Windows uses `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` (and avoids `SO_REUSEADDR`), so conflicts were detected and auto-increment worked. The Windows-appropriate fix is to use `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` instead of `SO_REUSEADDR` on Windows.

This is a bug/regression, not intended deprecation.

This is a confirmed **regression** (works in `1.58.0`, crashes in every version from `1.59.0` onward). When a fragment calls `.status()` on a container declared *outside* the fragment and then opens that status block with two separate `with` statements, the app crashes to a blank page with `Uncaught Error: Cannot set a node at a delta path`.

**Root cause** (matches the reporter's excellent analysis): `StatusContainer._create` captures the delta path from the **parent cursor before** the block is created (`lib/streamlit/elements/lib/mutable_status_container.py:81-91`). Since `1.59.0`, a write from a fragment into an outside container is redirected into a per-fragment layout-transparent wrapper block, so the status (`expandable`) block actually lands one level deeper than the captured path predicted. The stale `_delta_path` therefore points at the `transparent` wrapper instead of the status. On the second `with`, `__exit__` calls `update(state="complete")`, which re-emits the status block directly at that stale path (`mutable_status_container.py:151`). On the frontend, `AppRoot.addBlock` only inherits the existing children when the block type matches (`frontend/lib/src/render-tree/AppRoot.ts:467-483`); `transparent` ≠ `expandable`, so the whole subtree is dropped and the next element is written to a path whose parent no longer exists, causing `SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor` to throw. Note the one-`with` variant silently corrupts the tree without a visible crash.

A promising fix is to capture `_delta_path` **after** `_block()` from the path it actually wrote to, rather than predicting it from the parent cursor beforehand; other elements that store a delta path and later enqueue a message with it directly should be audited too.

### Related Issues

- [#12762](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12762) — "Key is ignored when using fragments and containers": exercises the same fragment-writing-into-an-outside-container code path (the redirection into a per-fragment wrapper introduced in 1.59.x), so widget/element identity gets misassigned across the fragment boundary.
- [#12514](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12514) — "Fragments within container disappearing on rerender": another element-tree corruption for fragments inside containers. The reporter references it directly; #16171 fixed #12514 but is present in the nightly that still reproduces this crash, confirming it is a distinct defect.
- [#13024](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13024) — "Make `st.fragment` behave correctly inside of `st.container`": describes the internal per-fragment layout wrapper block, which is the same transparent wrapper that misdirects the stored delta path here.

)

# Apply theme if changed

if selected_theme != st.session_state.current_theme:
    update_theme(themes[selected_theme])
    st.session_state.current_theme = selected_theme
    st.rerun()
```

This is a confirmed bug where the horizontal scrollbar in `st.dataframe` is visible but non-functional when using `width="content"` inside an `st.columns` layout. The dataframe's index column contains long text that overflows the column container, causing a native scrollbar to appear, but pointer interactions with the scrollbar are intercepted by the underlying GlideDataGrid component.

**Potential root cause:** The `measureTableScrollbars` function in `DataFrame.tsx` (lines 613–639) determines whether horizontal/vertical scrolling is active by comparing the `.dvn-stack` element's bounds against the container's `clientWidth`. When using `width="content"` inside a column (`isInHorizontalLayout=true`), the `StyledResizableContainer` uses `display: flex` with no explicit width constraint (`maxWidth: undefined` on the `Resizable` child). This can cause the measurement to incorrectly report `hasHorizontalScroll=false`. When `hasHorizontalScroll` is false, two things break: (1) the `onPointerDown` handler (lines 703–731) does not call `stopPropagation()` for clicks in the scrollbar area, allowing GlideDataGrid to capture those pointer events instead of the native scrollbar, and (2) the `experimental.paddingBottom` is not set to the negative scrollbar gutter, which may cause visual overlap issues. The GlideDataGrid config uses `scrollbarWidthOverride: 0`, meaning the grid treats the scrollbar region as part of its interactive area and captures mouse events there.

### Related Issues

- [#12683 — Dataframes with `width="content"` are not resizable](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12683): Directly related — another `width="content"` sizing bug where the resize handle is disabled, introduced as a regression. Both issues stem from the special handling of content-width dataframes in constrained layouts.
- [#12047 — Some suggestions for improving `dataframe`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12047): Filed by the same author, includes a request to remove unnecessary scrollbars in `st.dataframe`, which is the flip side of this bug (scrollbars appearing but not working).
- [#6784 — Dataframe scrollbars are too tiny](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6784): Related scrollbar usability issue in `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` — the overlay scrollbar approach (using `scrollbarWidthOverride: 0`) that contributes to this bug was likely introduced to address scrollbar styling concerns.

I attempted a fix for this and want to record measured findings, because they **rule out** the automated triage theory above and quantify why the obvious one-line fix makes things worse.

All numbers below are from Chromium via Playwright against current `develop`, using the exact repro from the issue body (long index, `width="content"`, inside `st.columns(2)`).

**1. The scrollbar detection is NOT broken.** The triage comment proposes that `measureTableScrollbars` wrongly reports `hasHorizontalScroll=false`, so `onPointerDown` never calls `stopPropagation()`. Measured geometry:

```
.dvn-stack width      = 550
container clientWidth = 344
canvas width          = 342
computed overflow-x   = visible
```

`measureTableScrollbars` computes `hasHorizontalScroll = scrollAreaBounds.width > clientWidth` → `550 > 344` → **true**. So detection works and the `stopPropagation()` path does run. That theory can be set aside.

**2. The real problem is that the grid is laid out 550px wide inside a 344px container, unclipped** (`overflow-x: visible`). glide-data-grid therefore believes its viewport is the full content width and has nothing to scroll internally, while the content visibly spills outside the column — which matches @lukasmasuch's read that the pinned index column ends up overlaying everything.

**3. The obvious fix makes it strictly worse, and the existing code comment is correct.** `DataFrame.tsx` currently has:

```js
// The maxWidth is not calculated correctly for content width
// dataframes in horizontal layouts, so it is disabled.
maxWidth={disableResize ? undefined : maxWidth}
```

Since `disableResize = isInHorizontalLayout || (useContent && !isInRoot)`, this passes `undefined` and lets the container grow to 550. Passing `maxWidth` unconditionally instead **collapses the dataframe to 52px**:

```
container clientWidth = 52   (was 344)
canvas width          = 50
```

52px is exactly `minColumnWidth + 2 * tableBorderWidth` = `round(3.125rem) + 2` = `50 + 2`. In `useTableSizer`, `availableWidth = Math.max(containerWidth, minWidth)`, so this proves `containerWidth <= 52` — i.e. **the measured container width is genuinely 0/-1 in this layout**, precisely as the `disableResize` comment says ("requires measurements from the parent container which cannot be determined when the parent container has a fit-content width").

So `maxWidth` is not merely disabled out of caution; it is unusable here because its input is missing.

**4. Where a real fix has to start.** Interestingly, the DOM *does* expose a usable width at measure time — the immediate parent and grandparent both reported `344`. So the information exists; it is the `containerWidth` plumbed into `useTableSizer` (via the `Block` resize observer) that degenerates for fit-content parents. A genuine fix means giving content-width dataframes a reliable available-width source in horizontal/fit-content layouts, then re-enabling `maxWidth`. That is a layout-measurement change rather than a local patch, so I did not want to guess at it — especially since it would also need to not regress the many other dataframe layout paths.

This is very likely the same root cause as **#12683** (`width="content"` dataframes not resizable): both are downstream of `disableResize` compensating for an unavailable container measurement. They may be worth fixing together.

I have not opened a PR, since the correct fix requires a direction decision on how to measure available width for fit-content parents.

Pressing `ESC` on an `st.multiselect` that has **no `default`** wipes the user's current selection instead of just dismissing the dropdown. This is a follow-up to #15637 / PR #15646, which only partially fixed the problem: the fix disables ESC-clearing when a default is provided, but leaves it enabled for multiselects without a default.

**Root cause:** `st.multiselect` renders BaseWeb's `Select`, whose `escapeClearsValue` prop defaults to `true`. In `frontend/lib/src/components/widgets/Multiselect/Multiselect.tsx` this is set conditionally:

```tsx
escapeClearsValue={element.default.length > 0 ? false : !disabled}
```

Because the condition only checks `element.default` (the initial default), a multiselect created without a default still has `escapeClearsValue = true`. So when a user manually selects options and presses `ESC` (once when the dropdown is closed, or after closing an open dropdown), BaseWeb clears the whole selection. This exactly matches the reporter's observation that ESC only preserves the selection when the widget is initialized with a non-empty default. This is a frontend-only behavior; the fix would be to make `escapeClearsValue={false}` unconditionally (as is already done for the `MultiSelectCell` in the data editor at `MultiSelectCell.tsx:534`), or otherwise decouple ESC-clearing from the presence of a default.

### Related Issues

- **#15637 – "pressing ESC clear the contents of multiselect"** (closed, same author): Direct predecessor of this report. It was closed by PR #15646, whose fix only covered the "has a default" case, so this issue is effectively a re-report for the "no default" case that remained broken.
- **#12260 – "Regression: Selectbox/Multiselect keyboard focus not activating on mobile"**: Another `st.multiselect` keyboard-interaction bug; related in that both concern keyboard handling of the multiselect widget (though a distinct symptom).
- **#12392 – "state management issues with st.pills ... selections get reset"**: Related theme of a selection widget unexpectedly clearing previously selected items, albeit for a different widget and trigger.

Thanks for the detailed repro, @clo-vis — we reproduced this on 1.60.0.

This is currently **intended behavior**: a widget created without a `default` is treated as "clearable," and pressing `ESC` on a clearable widget clears its value. This matches `st.selectbox` (a selectbox with no default also resets to empty on `ESC`). That's why PR #15646 — which fixed the *has-a-default* case from #15637 — deliberately left the no-default case clearing.

That said, we hear that ESC wiping a selection you built up manually is surprising, and our own data-editor multiselect never clears on ESC. We'll discuss internally whether to change this so ESC only dismisses the dropdown and never clears the selection.

### Summary

This is a `st.pills` bug (also applies to `st.segmented_control`, which shares the same `ButtonGroup` implementation): when `format_func` output for the currently-selected option changes between reruns (here the record count in the label changes as `df` is filtered), the pill visually appears **deselected**, even though `session_state` and the return value still hold the correct underlying value. The reporter's second example without `format_func` works, isolating `format_func` as the trigger.

### Potential root cause

Since the 1.54 refactor, these button-group widgets identify/track the selected option by its **formatted display string** rather than by the underlying value:

- Frontend (`frontend/lib/src/components/widgets/ButtonGroup/ButtonGroup.tsx`) stores the widget value as the formatted content string and highlights selection via `contentStringsToIndices(options, value)`. When `format_func` output changes (e.g. `"D (2)"` → `"D (3)"`), the stored string no longer matches any current option's content, so `selectedKeys` is empty and nothing renders as selected.
- Backend (`lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/button_group.py`) maps wire values via `formatted_option_to_option_index`, and only preserves the *value* through `session_state_fallback` — which is why `session_state`/the return value stay correct while the visual selection is lost.

Note there is already substantial handling for dynamic `format_func`/option changes in recent versions — the `session_state_fallback` + `set_value` re-serialization added in #15522 (shipped in 1.60.0) and the dynamic-options support in #13684. The report was filed without a version, so the team should confirm the exact Streamlit version and whether this still reproduces on the latest release; this may be a remaining edge case in the interdependent (parent→child) pills flow rather than a fully open regression.

### Related Issues

- [#12392](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12392) — State management issues with `st.pills` when options change dynamically based on a parent selection (selections get reset). Closest match: same widget and the same interdependent parent→child pattern.
- [#8008](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8008) — `st.selectbox` returns a stale value when `format_func` output changes; same root cause of using `format_func` output as the option identity/key.
- [#14115](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14115) — `st.radio` returns the wrong option because (since 1.54) options are identified by their formatted display text; same family of `format_func`-as-identity bugs.

This is a **bug**: `st.download_button` advertises `io.StringIO` as a supported `data` value (docstring, the public `DownloadButtonDataType` alias via `TextIO`, and the `button_types.py` typing test all accept it), but passing one raises `StreamlitAPIException: Invalid binary data format: <class '_io.StringIO'>` at runtime.

The root cause is in `convert_data_to_bytes_and_infer_mime` (`lib/streamlit/runtime/download_data_util.py`). It only handles text streams via `isinstance(data, io.TextIOWrapper)`, but `io.StringIO` is a *sibling* subclass of `io.TextIOBase` — it is **not** an `io.TextIOWrapper` — so it never matches the text branch (nor any `bytes`/`io.BytesIO`/`io.RawIOBase` branch) and falls through to `raise unsupported_error`. Because both the eager and deferred (callable) code paths in `button.py` route through this same helper, `io.StringIO` fails in both cases. The reporter's linked patch fixes this by reading `io.StringIO` via `getvalue()`, mirroring the existing `io.BytesIO` handling. A broader alternative would be to match `io.TextIOBase` so any text stream is covered.

### Related Issues

- [#14159 — st.download_button generate file_name and mime from io.FileIO](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14159): Also concerns how `st.download_button` handles file-like objects and MIME inference in the same `convert_data_to_bytes_and_infer_mime` code path; both point at gaps in the supported-`io.*`-types handling.
- [#5053 — Deferred data for download button](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5053): Introduced the deferred-callable path that shares the same data-conversion helper affected by this bug.

This issue reports that when a WebSocket connection closes uncleanly (e.g., due to network disruptions), Streamlit creates a new session instead of reconnecting to the existing one, causing users to lose their session state.

**Root cause analysis:** The issue originates in `lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py` in the `connect_session()` method. When a client attempts to reconnect with an existing session ID, the code checks if that session is already in `_active_session_info_by_id` (line 103). If it is, a warning is logged ("Session with id %s is already connected!") and a **new** session is created instead. The session can only be restored from storage if it's NOT currently active.

The core problem is a race condition: on an unclean WebSocket close, the server may not have detected the disconnect yet, so the session remains "active" in memory. When the client quickly reconnects with the same session ID, the server sees it as "already connected" and creates a new session instead of allowing reconnection. A potential fix would need to handle this case by either closing the existing connection first, implementing a grace period, or using a different strategy for tracking active vs. disconnected sessions.

### Related Issues

1. **[#9031](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9031)** - "Current recommended way to deal with restarted Streamlit sessions" - Directly related issue where users request better session recovery mechanisms after unexpected restarts.

2. **[#11012](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11012)** - "Preserve session state (e.g. in file, database, or localstorage)" - Related enhancement request for persisting session state across browser sessions, which would help mitigate the impact of session loss.

3. **[#12108](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12108)** - "Frequent websocket connection drops on higher ping_interval" - Related WebSocket stability issue that can trigger the reconnection problem described in this issue.

Thanks for the detailed report! This looks like a regression introduced in **v1.57.0**, which switched the default (and only) web server from Tornado to **Starlette + Uvicorn** (#14553). The traceback originates inside `websockets/legacy/protocol.py` (the WebSocket library that Uvicorn uses by default — see `_get_uvicorn_config_kwargs` in `lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_server.py`, where `"ws": "auto"` is set), and bubbles up through `asyncio/proactor_events.py` and `asyncio/windows_events.py`.

`OSError: [WinError 121] The semaphore timeout period has expired` is a Windows-specific OS-level error raised by overlapped I/O on the `ProactorEventLoop` when a socket read times out (typically a transient network condition or an idle/half-open connection). With the previous Tornado-based server, this same OS condition was handled silently inside Tornado's WebSocket read loop, so it never surfaced as a logged traceback. Under Uvicorn + the legacy `websockets` reader, the exception propagates up to `transfer_data` and is logged as `data transfer failed`, even though the connection is then closed cleanly and the client transparently reconnects (which matches the reporter's observation that there is no visible UI disruption).

So the impact is most likely **noise in the logs only**, but it is a behavior change vs. 1.56.0 and worth investigating — possibly by catching/quieting transient `OSError` on the websocket read path, switching to the non-legacy `websockets` implementation / `wsproto`, or revisiting whether to set the Windows event loop policy explicitly.

### Related Issues

- [#14991](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/14991) — Another v1.57.0 regression directly caused by the same Tornado → Starlette/Uvicorn migration (OAuth `MismatchingStateError`). Strong sibling of this issue, both rooted in #14553.
- [#12108](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12108) — Frequent WebSocket connection drops tied to `websocket_ping_interval`/`ping_timeout` behavior. Closely related, since this issue may also be sensitive to the new Uvicorn ping settings (`ws_ping_interval` / `ws_ping_timeout` configured in `_get_uvicorn_config_kwargs`).
- [#7825](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7825) — Tracks the asyncio event loop policy choice on Windows (Selector vs. Proactor). Relevant because the traceback here goes through `ProactorEventLoop`, and the event-loop choice could be part of the fix or workaround.

<details>
<summary>Claude analysis on this issue</summary>

# Summary                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                         
  This is a **bug in the components v2 `manifest_scanner.py`**, not specifically Starlette's fault.                      
                                                                                                                         
  ## The Issue                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                         
  Looking at `lib/streamlit/components/v2/manifest_scanner.py:191`:                                                      
                                                                                                                         
  ```python                                                                                                              
  def _is_likely_streamlit_component_package(                                                                            
      dist: importlib.metadata.Distribution,                                                                             
  ) -> bool:                                                                                                             
      # ...                                                                                                              
      name = dist.name.lower()  # <-- BUG: dist.name can be None                                                         
  ```                                                                                                                       
  The dist.name attribute from importlib.metadata.Distribution can be None in edge cases:                                
                                                                                                                         
  - Corrupted or malformed package metadata                                                                              
  - Certain editable installs                                                                                            
  - Packages installed in unusual ways                                                                                   
                                                                                                                         
  When dist.name is None, calling .lower() on it throws:                                                                 
                                                                                                                         
  'NoneType' object has no attribute 'lower'                                                                             
                                                                                                                         
  Why Starlette Triggers It                                                                                              
                                                                                                                         
  Starlette itself isn't the problem, but it likely:                                                                     
                                                                                                                         
  1. Has a dependency installed in a way that produces a distribution with None name                                     
  2. Or one of its transitive dependencies has malformed metadata                                                        
                                                                                                                         
  The scan iterates over all installed distributions via importlib.metadata.distributions(), so any broken package in the
   environment can trigger this.                                                                                         
                                                                                                                         
  The Fix                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                         
  The code should guard against None before calling .lower(). A simple fix would be:                                     
   
  ```python                                                                                                              
  def _is_likely_streamlit_component_package(                                                                            
      dist: importlib.metadata.Distribution,                                                                             
  ) -> bool:                                                                                                             
      # Skip distributions without a name                                                                                
      if dist.name is None:                                                                                              
          return False                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                         
      name = dist.name.lower()                                                                                           
      # ...                                                                                                              
 ```
                                                                                                     
  There are also other places in the file that use dist.name (lines 238, 510) that should be similarly guarded, though   
  they're only reached after the filtering function passes, so fixing line 191 would prevent most issues. 

</details>
